# Orbit CLI reference
Orbit builds, deploys and runs web applications. This page documents every command of the orbit CLI, version 3.8. Install it with curl -fsSL https://get.orbit.example | sh or brew install orbit .
## Commands
Every command accepts --help , --json for machine-readable output and --quiet to print only errors.
### orbit init
Create an orbit.toml in the current directory and link it to a project.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--name
directory name
Project name shown in the dashboard.
--region
eu-west
Default region for new environments.
--template
none
Start from a template: static , node or rust .
Example:
orbit init --name shop --region us-east
### orbit build
Build the project into an immutable artifact. Builds run in a clean container and are cached by the hash of your lockfiles.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--timeout
300 seconds
Abort the build after this long.
--no-cache
off
Ignore cached layers.
--target
release
Build profile: release or debug .
--arg KEY=VALUE
none
Pass a build argument. Repeatable.
Example:
orbit build --target debug --arg API_URL=https://api.example.com
### orbit deploy
Upload the latest artifact and roll it out to an environment. Traffic shifts to the new release once every instance passes its health check.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to deploy to.
--timeout
90 seconds
How long to wait for health checks before the deploy fails and traffic stays on the previous release.
--strategy
rolling
rolling , blue-green or canary .
--canary-percent
10
Share of traffic for a canary release.
--message
none
A note stored with the release.
Example:
orbit deploy --env production --timeout 180 --strategy blue-green
### orbit rollback
Move traffic back to an earlier release of the same environment. No rebuild happens: the old artifact is reused.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to roll back.
--to
previous release
Release id to return to, as shown by orbit releases .
Example:
orbit rollback --env production --to r-2041
### orbit releases
List the releases of an environment, newest first, with their id, author, message and status.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to list.
--limit
20
How many releases to show.
Example:
orbit releases --env production --limit 5
### orbit logs
Stream logs from every instance of an environment.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to read.
--since
15m
Start this far back, e.g. 2h .
--follow
off
Keep streaming new lines.
--grep
none
Only lines matching a regular expression.
Example:
orbit logs --env production --since 1h --grep timeout
### orbit test
Run the project's test command in the same container image as the build.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--timeout
120 seconds
Abort the test run after this long.
--shard
1/1
Run one shard of the suite, e.g. 2/4 .
Example:
orbit test --shard 1/3
### orbit env
Create, list and delete environments.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
create NAME
—
Create an environment.
list
—
List environments and their current release.
delete NAME
—
Delete an environment and its releases. Asks for confirmation.
Example:
orbit env create preview-42
### orbit secrets
Manage encrypted secrets. Secrets are injected as environment variables at runtime and never appear in build logs.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
set KEY VALUE
—
Create or replace a secret.
unset KEY
—
Remove a secret.
list
—
List secret names (never values).
--env
all environments
Limit to one environment.
Example:
orbit secrets set STRIPE_KEY sk_live_... --env production
### orbit domains
Attach custom domains. Orbit provisions TLS certificates automatically once DNS points to your environment.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
add DOMAIN
—
Attach a domain.
remove DOMAIN
—
Detach a domain.
verify DOMAIN
—
Check DNS and certificate status.
Example:
orbit domains add shop.example.com --env production
### orbit scale
Change the number and size of instances.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to scale.
--instances
2
Instance count, 1 to 50.
--size
small
small (0.5 vCPU, 512 MB), medium (1 vCPU, 2 GB) or large (4 vCPU, 8 GB).
Example:
orbit scale --env production --instances 6 --size medium
### orbit login
Authenticate this machine. Opens a browser window; on headless machines, prints a one-time code instead.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--token
none
Use an access token instead of the browser flow (for CI).
Example:
orbit login --token $ORBIT_TOKEN
## Configuration file
Orbit reads orbit.toml from the current directory or the nearest parent directory. Keys use dotted names below; in the file they live under [build] , [deploy] and [runtime] tables.
Key
Type
Default
Description
project
string
required
Project name.
region
string
"eu-west"
Default region.
build.command
string
auto-detected
Command that produces the artifact.
build.output
path
"dist"
Directory packaged as the artifact.
deploy.health_check
path
"/healthz"
Path that must return 2xx before traffic shifts.
deploy.retain_releases
integer
10
How many past releases are kept for rollback. Older releases are deleted and can no longer be rolled back to.
deploy.strategy
string
"rolling"
Default rollout strategy.
runtime.port
integer
8080
Port your server listens on.
runtime.max_body
size
"10 MB"
Largest accepted request body.
project = "shop" region = "us-east" [deploy] health_check = "/ready" retain_releases = 25
## Environment variables
Variable
Effect
ORBIT_TOKEN
Access token for non-interactive use. Overrides the credentials saved by orbit login .
ORBIT_HOME
Directory for Orbit's cache and credentials. Default: ~/.orbit .
ORBIT_CONFIG
Path to the project config file, instead of looking for orbit.toml in the current directory and its parents.
ORBIT_REGION
Region used when neither a flag nor the config sets one.
ORBIT_NO_COLOR
Disable colored output. NO_COLOR is honored too.
ORBIT_LOG
CLI log level: error , warn , info or debug .
Flags win over environment variables, which win over orbit.toml .
## Exit codes
Code
Meaning
0
Success.
1
Generic failure; see the message.
2
Invalid usage: unknown command, flag or value.
3
Not authenticated. Run orbit login or set ORBIT_TOKEN .
4
Quota exceeded: your plan's build minutes or instance limit is used up. Upgrade the plan or wait for the monthly reset.
5
Health checks did not pass within the deploy timeout; traffic stayed on the previous release.
6
Network error talking to the Orbit API. Safe to retry.
7
The release or environment was not found.
## Frequently asked questions
### Why is my build slower than locally?
Builds start from a clean container. The first build of a branch fills the cache; later builds reuse layers unless your lockfiles change. Use --no-cache only when debugging cache problems.
### Can I deploy without building?
No. Every deploy points at an artifact produced by orbit build , which keeps releases reproducible. Rollbacks are the exception: they reuse an old artifact.
### How do preview environments work?
Create one per pull request with orbit env create preview-<n> and delete it when the pull request closes. Preview environments count toward your instance quota.
### Where are secrets stored?
Secrets are encrypted at rest with a per-project key and decrypted only inside your instances. Orbit staff cannot read secret values.
### How do I see who deployed?
Run orbit releases ; every release records its author and message.
### Does Orbit support WebSockets?
Yes, on all strategies. During a rolling deploy, existing connections stay on old instances until they close or 10 minutes pass.
## Changelog
3.8 : Canary deploys gain --canary-percent .
3.7 : orbit logs --grep .
3.6 : Default deploy timeout raised from 60 to 90 seconds.
3.5 : deploy.retain_releases default raised from 5 to 10.
3.4 : Blue-green deploys.
© Orbit Platform ·

# Orbit CLI reference
Orbit builds, deploys and runs web applications. This page documents every command of the orbit CLI, version 3.8. Install it with curl -fsSL https://get.orbit.example | sh or brew install orbit .
## Commands
Every command accepts --help , --json for machine-readable output and --quiet to print only errors.
### orbit init
Create an orbit.toml in the current directory and link it to a project.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--name
directory name
Project name shown in the dashboard.
--region
eu-west
Default region for new environments.
--template
none
Start from a template: static , node or rust .
Example:
orbit init --name shop --region us-east
### orbit build
Build the project into an immutable artifact. Builds run in a clean container and are cached by the hash of your lockfiles.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--timeout
300 seconds
Abort the build after this long.
--no-cache
off
Ignore cached layers.
--target
release
Build profile: release or debug .
--arg KEY=VALUE
none
Pass a build argument. Repeatable.
Example:
orbit build --target debug --arg API_URL=https://api.example.com
### orbit deploy
Upload the latest artifact and roll it out to an environment. Traffic shifts to the new release once every instance passes its health check.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to deploy to.
--timeout
90 seconds
How long to wait for health checks before the deploy fails and traffic stays on the previous release.
--strategy
rolling
rolling , blue-green or canary .
--canary-percent
10
Share of traffic for a canary release.
--message
none
A note stored with the release.
Example:
orbit deploy --env production --timeout 180 --strategy blue-green
### orbit rollback
Move traffic back to an earlier release of the same environment. No rebuild happens: the old artifact is reused.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to roll back.
--to
previous release
Release id to return to, as shown by orbit releases .
Example:
orbit rollback --env production --to r-2041
### orbit releases
List the releases of an environment, newest first, with their id, author, message and status.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to list.
--limit
20
How many releases to show.
Example:
orbit releases --env production --limit 5
### orbit logs
Stream logs from every instance of an environment.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to read.
--since
15m
Start this far back, e.g. 2h .
--follow
off
Keep streaming new lines.
--grep
none
Only lines matching a regular expression.
Example:
orbit logs --env production --since 1h --grep timeout
### orbit test
Run the project's test command in the same container image as the build.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--timeout
120 seconds
Abort the test run after this long.
--shard
1/1
Run one shard of the suite, e.g. 2/4 .
Example:
orbit test --shard 1/3
### orbit env
Create, list and delete environments.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
create NAME
—
Create an environment.
list
—
List environments and their current release.
delete NAME
—
Delete an environment and its releases. Asks for confirmation.
Example:
orbit env create preview-42
### orbit secrets
Manage encrypted secrets. Secrets are injected as environment variables at runtime and never appear in build logs.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
set KEY VALUE
—
Create or replace a secret.
unset KEY
—
Remove a secret.
list
—
List secret names (never values).
--env
all environments
Limit to one environment.
Example:
orbit secrets set STRIPE_KEY sk_live_... --env production
### orbit domains
Attach custom domains. Orbit provisions TLS certificates automatically once DNS points to your environment.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
add DOMAIN
—
Attach a domain.
remove DOMAIN
—
Detach a domain.
verify DOMAIN
—
Check DNS and certificate status.
Example:
orbit domains add shop.example.com --env production
### orbit scale
Change the number and size of instances.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--env
staging
Environment to scale.
--instances
2
Instance count, 1 to 50.
--size
small
small (0.5 vCPU, 512 MB), medium (1 vCPU, 2 GB) or large (4 vCPU, 8 GB).
Example:
orbit scale --env production --instances 6 --size medium
### orbit login
Authenticate this machine. Opens a browser window; on headless machines, prints a one-time code instead.
Flag or subcommand
Default
Description
--token
none
Use an access token instead of the browser flow (for CI).
Example:
orbit login --token $ORBIT_TOKEN
## Configuration file
Orbit reads orbit.toml from the current directory or the nearest parent directory. Keys use dotted names below; in the file they live under [build] , [deploy] and [runtime] tables.
Key
Type
Default
Description
project
string
required
Project name.
region
string
"eu-west"
Default region.
build.command
string
auto-detected
Command that produces the artifact.
build.output
path
"dist"
Directory packaged as the artifact.
deploy.health_check
path
"/healthz"
Path that must return 2xx before traffic shifts.
deploy.retain_releases
integer
10
How many past releases are kept for rollback. Older releases are deleted and can no longer be rolled back to.
deploy.strategy
string
"rolling"
Default rollout strategy.
runtime.port
integer
8080
Port your server listens on.
runtime.max_body
size
"10 MB"
Largest accepted request body.
project = "shop" region = "us-east" [deploy] health_check = "/ready" retain_releases = 25
## Environment variables
Variable
Effect
ORBIT_TOKEN
Access token for non-interactive use. Overrides the credentials saved by orbit login .
ORBIT_HOME
Directory for Orbit's cache and credentials. Default: ~/.orbit .
ORBIT_CONFIG
Path to the project config file, instead of looking for orbit.toml in the current directory and its parents.
ORBIT_REGION
Region used when neither a flag nor the config sets one.
ORBIT_NO_COLOR
Disable colored output. NO_COLOR is honored too.
ORBIT_LOG
CLI log level: error , warn , info or debug .
Flags win over environment variables, which win over orbit.toml .
## Exit codes
Code
Meaning
0
Success.
1
Generic failure; see the message.
2
Invalid usage: unknown command, flag or value.
3
Not authenticated. Run orbit login or set ORBIT_TOKEN .
4
Quota exceeded: your plan's build minutes or instance limit is used up. Upgrade the plan or wait for the monthly reset.
5
Health checks did not pass within the deploy timeout; traffic stayed on the previous release.
6
Network error talking to the Orbit API. Safe to retry.
7
The release or environment was not found.
## Frequently asked questions
### Why is my build slower than locally?
Builds start from a clean container. The first build of a branch fills the cache; later builds reuse layers unless your lockfiles change. Use --no-cache only when debugging cache problems.
### Can I deploy without building?
No. Every deploy points at an artifact produced by orbit build , which keeps releases reproducible. Rollbacks are the exception: they reuse an old artifact.
### How do preview environments work?
Create one per pull request with orbit env create preview-<n> and delete it when the pull request closes. Preview environments count toward your instance quota.
### Where are secrets stored?
Secrets are encrypted at rest with a per-project key and decrypted only inside your instances. Orbit staff cannot read secret values.
### How do I see who deployed?
Run orbit releases ; every release records its author and message.
### Does Orbit support WebSockets?
Yes, on all strategies. During a rolling deploy, existing connections stay on old instances until they close or 10 minutes pass.
## Changelog
3.8 : Canary deploys gain --canary-percent .
3.7 : orbit logs --grep .
3.6 : Default deploy timeout raised from 60 to 90 seconds.
3.5 : deploy.retain_releases default raised from 5 to 10.
3.4 : Blue-green deploys.

Builds start from a clean container. The first build of a branch fills the cache; later builds reuse layers unless your lockfiles change. Use --no-cache only when debugging cache problems.

### orbit init

10

Variable
Effect

ORBIT_HOME

Code
Meaning
0
Success.
1
Generic failure; see the message.
2
Invalid usage: unknown command, flag or value.
3
Not authenticated. Run orbit login or set ORBIT_TOKEN .
4
Quota exceeded: your plan's build minutes or instance limit is used up. Upgrade the plan or wait for the monthly reset.
5
Health checks did not pass within the deploy timeout; traffic stayed on the previous release.
6
Network error talking to the Orbit API. Safe to retry.
7
The release or environment was not found.
## Frequently asked questions
### Why is my build slower than locally?
Builds start from a clean container. The first build of a branch fills the cache; later builds reuse layers unless your lockfiles change. Use --no-cache only when debugging cache problems.
### Can I deploy without building?
No. Every deploy points at an artifact produced by orbit build , which keeps releases reproducible. Rollbacks are the exception: they reuse an old artifact.
### How do preview environments work?
Create one per pull request with orbit env create preview-<n> and delete it when the pull request closes. Preview environments count toward your instance quota.
### Where are secrets stored?
Secrets are encrypted at rest with a per-project key and decrypted only inside your instances. Orbit staff cannot read secret values.
### How do I see who deployed?
Run orbit releases ; every release records its author and message.
### Does Orbit support WebSockets?
Yes, on all strategies. During a rolling deploy, existing connections stay on old instances until they close or 10 minutes pass.

3.7 : orbit logs --grep .
3.6 : Default deploy timeout raised from 60 to 90 seconds.
3.5 : deploy.retain_releases default raised from 5 to 10.

Meaning

Builds start from a clean container. The first build of a branch fills the cache; later builds reuse layers unless your lockfiles change. Use --no-cache only when debugging cache problems.

## Frequently Asked Questions
[90] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#frequently-asked-questions
Frequently asked questions related to D1 limits:
### How much work can a D1 database do?
[91] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#how-much-work-can-a-d1-database-do
D1 is designed for horizontal scale out across multiple, smaller (10 GB) databases, such as per-user, per-tenant or per-entity databases. The Workers Paid plan includes 100,000 databases per account. You pay
[92] link "$0.10 per D1 database per month" -> /d1/platform/pricing/#billing-metrics
above the included amount. Query and storage charges apply separately.
#### Storage
[93] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#storage
Each D1 database can store up to 10 GB of data.
Caution
Note that the 10 GB limit of a D1 database cannot be further increased.
#### Concurrency and throughput
[94] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#concurrency-and-throughput
Each individual D1 database is inherently single-threaded, and processes queries one at a time.
Your maximum throughput is directly related to the duration of your queries.
If your average query takes 1 ms, you can run at most 1,000 queries per second.
If your average query takes 100 ms, you can run at most 10 queries per second.
Note that there is a small overhead per request that is not included in the timings that D1 reports. As a result, a database receiving many small requests would reach its limit before 1 / query duration requests per second.
To get more throughput from a single database, reduce the number of requests rather than only the duration of each query. For example, use
[95] link "batch()" -> /d1/worker-api/d1-database/#batch
to send multiple statements in a single request, so that the per-request overhead is paid once for the whole batch.
A database that receives too many concurrent requests will first attempt to queue them. If the queue becomes full, the database will return an
[96] link ""overloaded" error" -> /d1/observability/debug-d1/#error-list
.
Each individual D1 database is backed by a single
[97] link "Durable Object" -> /durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/
. When using
[98] link "D1 read replication ↗︎" -> /d1/best-practices/read-replication/#primary-database-instance-vs-read-replicas
each replica instance is a different Durable Object and the guidelines apply to each replica instance independently.
#### Query performance
[99] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#query-performance
Query performance is the most important factor for throughput. As a rough guideline:
Read queries like SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ? with an appropriate index on id will take less than a millisecond for SQL duration.
Write queries like INSERT or UPDATE can take several milliseconds for SQL duration, and depend on the number of rows written. Writes need to be durably persisted across several locations - learn more on
[100] link "how D1 persists data under the hood ↗︎" -> https://blog.cloudflare.com/d1-read-replication-beta/#under-the-hood-how-d1-read-replication-is-implemented
.
Data migrations like a large UPDATE or DELETE affecting millions of rows must be run in batches. A single query that attempts to modify hundreds of thousands of rows or hundreds of MBs of data at once will exceed execution limits. Break the work into smaller chunks (e.g., processing 1,000 rows at a time) to stay within platform limits.
To ensure your queries are fast and efficient,
[101] link "use appropriate indexes in your SQL schema" -> /d1/best-practices/use-indexes/
.
#### CPU and memory
[102] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#cpu-and-memory
Operations on a D1 database, including query execution and result serialization, run within the
[103] link "Workers platform CPU and memory limits" -> /workers/platform/limits/#memory
.
Exceeding these limits, or hitting other platform limits, will generate errors. Refer to the
[104] link "D1 error list for more details" -> /d1/observability/debug-d1/#error-list
.
### How many simultaneous connections can a Worker open to D1?
[105] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#how-many-simultaneous-connections-can-a-worker-open-to-d1
You can open up to six connections (to D1) simultaneously for each invocation of your Worker.
For more information on a Worker's simultaneous connections, refer to
[106] link "Simultaneous open connections" -> /workers/platform/limits/#simultaneous-open-connections
.

Create new serverless SQL databases to query from your Workers and Pages projects.
Available on Free and Paid plans
D1 is Cloudflare's managed, serverless database with SQLite's SQL semantics, built-in disaster recovery, and Worker and HTTP API access.
D1 supports separate databases for users, tenants, or projects. The Workers Paid plan includes 100,000 databases. Additional databases cost $0.10 per database per month, alongside

## Frequently Asked Questions
[90] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#frequently-asked-questions
Frequently asked questions related to D1 limits:
### How much work can a D1 database do?
[91] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#how-much-work-can-a-d1-database-do
D1 is designed for horizontal scale out across multiple, smaller (10 GB) databases, such as per-user, per-tenant or per-entity databases. The Workers Paid plan includes 100,000 databases per account. You pay
[92] link "$0.10 per D1 database per month" -> /d1/platform/pricing/#billing-metrics
above the included amount. Query and storage charges apply separately.
#### Storage
[93] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#storage
Each D1 database can store up to 10 GB of data.
Caution
Note that the 10 GB limit of a D1 database cannot be further increased.
#### Concurrency and throughput
[94] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#concurrency-and-throughput
Each individual D1 database is inherently single-threaded, and processes queries one at a time.
Your maximum throughput is directly related to the duration of your queries.
If your average query takes 1 ms, you can run at most 1,000 queries per second.
If your average query takes 100 ms, you can run at most 10 queries per second.
Note that there is a small overhead per request that is not included in the timings that D1 reports. As a result, a database receiving many small requests would reach its limit before 1 / query duration requests per second.
To get more throughput from a single database, reduce the number of requests rather than only the duration of each query. For example, use
[95] link "batch()" -> /d1/worker-api/d1-database/#batch
to send multiple statements in a single request, so that the per-request overhead is paid once for the whole batch.
A database that receives too many concurrent requests will first attempt to queue them. If the queue becomes full, the database will return an
[96] link ""overloaded" error" -> /d1/observability/debug-d1/#error-list
.
Each individual D1 database is backed by a single
[97] link "Durable Object" -> /durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/
. When using
[98] link "D1 read replication ↗︎" -> /d1/best-practices/read-replication/#primary-database-instance-vs-read-replicas
each replica instance is a different Durable Object and the guidelines apply to each replica instance independently.
#### Query performance
[99] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#query-performance
Query performance is the most important factor for throughput. As a rough guideline:
Read queries like SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ? with an appropriate index on id will take less than a millisecond for SQL duration.
Write queries like INSERT or UPDATE can take several milliseconds for SQL duration, and depend on the number of rows written. Writes need to be durably persisted across several locations - learn more on
[100] link "how D1 persists data under the hood ↗︎" -> https://blog.cloudflare.com/d1-read-replication-beta/#under-the-hood-how-d1-read-replication-is-implemented
.
Data migrations like a large UPDATE or DELETE affecting millions of rows must be run in batches. A single query that attempts to modify hundreds of thousands of rows or hundreds of MBs of data at once will exceed execution limits. Break the work into smaller chunks (e.g., processing 1,000 rows at a time) to stay within platform limits.
To ensure your queries are fast and efficient,
[101] link "use appropriate indexes in your SQL schema" -> /d1/best-practices/use-indexes/
.
#### CPU and memory
[102] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#cpu-and-memory
Operations on a D1 database, including query execution and result serialization, run within the
[103] link "Workers platform CPU and memory limits" -> /workers/platform/limits/#memory
.
Exceeding these limits, or hitting other platform limits, will generate errors. Refer to the
[104] link "D1 error list for more details" -> /d1/observability/debug-d1/#error-list
.
### How many simultaneous connections can a Worker open to D1?
[105] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#how-many-simultaneous-connections-can-a-worker-open-to-d1
You can open up to six connections (to D1) simultaneously for each invocation of your Worker.
For more information on a Worker's simultaneous connections, refer to
[106] link "Simultaneous open connections" -> /workers/platform/limits/#simultaneous-open-connections
.

## Frequently Asked Questions
[90] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#frequently-asked-questions
Frequently asked questions related to D1 limits:
### How much work can a D1 database do?
[91] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#how-much-work-can-a-d1-database-do
D1 is designed for horizontal scale out across multiple, smaller (10 GB) databases, such as per-user, per-tenant or per-entity databases. The Workers Paid plan includes 100,000 databases per account. You pay
[92] link "$0.10 per D1 database per month" -> /d1/platform/pricing/#billing-metrics
above the included amount. Query and storage charges apply separately.
#### Storage
[93] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#storage
Each D1 database can store up to 10 GB of data.
Caution
Note that the 10 GB limit of a D1 database cannot be further increased.
#### Concurrency and throughput
[94] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#concurrency-and-throughput
Each individual D1 database is inherently single-threaded, and processes queries one at a time.
Your maximum throughput is directly related to the duration of your queries.
If your average query takes 1 ms, you can run at most 1,000 queries per second.
If your average query takes 100 ms, you can run at most 10 queries per second.
Note that there is a small overhead per request that is not included in the timings that D1 reports. As a result, a database receiving many small requests would reach its limit before 1 / query duration requests per second.
To get more throughput from a single database, reduce the number of requests rather than only the duration of each query. For example, use
[95] link "batch()" -> /d1/worker-api/d1-database/#batch
to send multiple statements in a single request, so that the per-request overhead is paid once for the whole batch.
A database that receives too many concurrent requests will first attempt to queue them. If the queue becomes full, the database will return an
[96] link ""overloaded" error" -> /d1/observability/debug-d1/#error-list
.
Each individual D1 database is backed by a single
[97] link "Durable Object" -> /durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/
. When using
[98] link "D1 read replication ↗︎" -> /d1/best-practices/read-replication/#primary-database-instance-vs-read-replicas
each replica instance is a different Durable Object and the guidelines apply to each replica instance independently.
#### Query performance
[99] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#query-performance
Query performance is the most important factor for throughput. As a rough guideline:
Read queries like SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ? with an appropriate index on id will take less than a millisecond for SQL duration.
Write queries like INSERT or UPDATE can take several milliseconds for SQL duration, and depend on the number of rows written. Writes need to be durably persisted across several locations - learn more on
[100] link "how D1 persists data under the hood ↗︎" -> https://blog.cloudflare.com/d1-read-replication-beta/#under-the-hood-how-d1-read-replication-is-implemented
.
Data migrations like a large UPDATE or DELETE affecting millions of rows must be run in batches. A single query that attempts to modify hundreds of thousands of rows or hundreds of MBs of data at once will exceed execution limits. Break the work into smaller chunks (e.g., processing 1,000 rows at a time) to stay within platform limits.
To ensure your queries are fast and efficient,
[101] link "use appropriate indexes in your SQL schema" -> /d1/best-practices/use-indexes/
.
#### CPU and memory
[102] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#cpu-and-memory
Operations on a D1 database, including query execution and result serialization, run within the
[103] link "Workers platform CPU and memory limits" -> /workers/platform/limits/#memory
.
Exceeding these limits, or hitting other platform limits, will generate errors. Refer to the
[104] link "D1 error list for more details" -> /d1/observability/debug-d1/#error-list
.
### How many simultaneous connections can a Worker open to D1?
[105] link "" -> /d1/platform/limits/#how-many-simultaneous-connections-can-a-worker-open-to-d1
You can open up to six connections (to D1) simultaneously for each invocation of your Worker.
For more information on a Worker's simultaneous connections, refer to
[106] link "Simultaneous open connections" -> /workers/platform/limits/#simultaneous-open-connections
.

Create a global, low-latency, key-value data storage.
Available on Free and Paid plans
Workers KV is a data storage that allows you to store and retrieve data globally. With Workers KV, you can build dynamic and performant APIs and websites that support high read volumes with low latency.
For example, you can use Workers KV for:
Caching API responses.
Storing user configurations / preferences.
Storing user authentication details.
Access your Workers KV namespace from Cloudflare Workers using

Create a global, low-latency, key-value data storage.
Available on Free and Paid plans
Workers KV is a data storage that allows you to store and retrieve data globally. With Workers KV, you can build dynamic and performant APIs and websites that support high read volumes with low latency.
For example, you can use Workers KV for:
Caching API responses.
Storing user configurations / preferences.
Storing user authentication details.
Access your Workers KV namespace from Cloudflare Workers using

or from your external application using the REST API:

Create a global, low-latency, key-value data storage.
Available on Free and Paid plans
Workers KV is a data storage that allows you to store and retrieve data globally. With Workers KV, you can build dynamic and performant APIs and websites that support high read volumes with low latency.
For example, you can use Workers KV for:
Caching API responses.
Storing user configurations / preferences.
Storing user authentication details.
Access your Workers KV namespace from Cloudflare Workers using
[62] link "Workers Bindings" -> /workers/runtime-apis/bindings/
or from your external application using the REST API:

Create a global, low-latency, key-value data storage.
Available on Free and Paid plans
Workers KV is a data storage that allows you to store and retrieve data globally. With Workers KV, you can build dynamic and performant APIs and websites that support high read volumes with low latency.
For example, you can use Workers KV for:
Caching API responses.
Storing user configurations / preferences.
Storing user authentication details.

Create a global, low-latency, key-value data storage.
Available on Free and Paid plans
Workers KV is a data storage that allows you to store and retrieve data globally. With Workers KV, you can build dynamic and performant APIs and websites that support high read volumes with low latency.
For example, you can use Workers KV for:
Caching API responses.
Storing user configurations / preferences.
Storing user authentication details.

By default, the maximum CPU time per consumer Worker invocation is set to 30 seconds, but can be increased by setting limits.cpu_ms in your Wrangler configuration:
[81] tab "wrangler.jsonc"
[82] tab "wrangler.toml"
{ // ...rest of your configuration... "limits" : { "cpu_ms" : 300000 , // 300,000 milliseconds = 5 minutes }, // ...rest of your configuration... }
[83] button "Copy code to clipboard"
To learn more about CPU time and limits,
[84] link "review the Workers documentation" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
.
## Wall time limits by invocation type
[85] link "" -> /queues/platform/limits/#wall-time-limits-by-invocation-type
Wall time (also called wall-clock time) is the total elapsed time from the start to end of an invocation, including time spent waiting on network requests, I/O, and other asynchronous operations. This is distinct from
[86] link "CPU time" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
, which only measures time the CPU spends actively executing your code.
The following table summarizes the wall time limits for different types of Worker invocations across the developer platform:
Invocation type
Wall time limit
Details
Incoming HTTP request
Unlimited
No hard limit while the client remains connected. Workers requests are subject to the
[87] link "grace period for runtime updates" -> /workers/platform/limits/#runtime-updates
. A Worker that is still streaming a response body remains active.
[88] link "waitUntil()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/context/#waituntil
extends execution for up to 30 seconds after the response or disconnect.
[89] link "Cron Triggers" -> /workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
15 minutes
Scheduled Workers have a maximum wall time of 15 minutes per invocation.
[90] link "Queue consumers" -> /queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer
15 minutes
Each consumer invocation has a maximum wall time of 15 minutes.
[91] link "Durable Object alarm handlers" -> /durable-objects/api/alarms/
15 minutes
Alarm handler invocations have a maximum wall time of 15 minutes.
[92] link "Durable Objects" -> /durable-objects/
(RPC / HTTP)
Unlimited
No hard limit while the caller stays connected to the Durable Object. Durable Objects remain active while a request, RPC call, response stream, WebSocket, or pending I/O is in flight.
[93] link "Workflows" -> /workflows/
(per step)
Unlimited
Each step can run for an unlimited wall time. Individual steps are subject to the configured
[94] link "CPU time limit" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time

### Increasing Queue Consumer Worker CPU Limits
[78] link "" -> /queues/platform/limits/#increasing-queue-consumer-worker-cpu-limits
[79] link "Queue consumer Workers" -> /queues/reference/how-queues-works/#consumers
are Worker scripts, and share the same
[80] link "per invocation CPU limits" -> /workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits
as any Workers do. Note that CPU time is active processing time: not time spent waiting on network requests, storage calls, or other general I/O.
By default, the maximum CPU time per consumer Worker invocation is set to 30 seconds, but can be increased by setting limits.cpu_ms in your Wrangler configuration:
[81] tab "wrangler.jsonc"
[82] tab "wrangler.toml"
{ // ...rest of your configuration... "limits" : { "cpu_ms" : 300000 , // 300,000 milliseconds = 5 minutes }, // ...rest of your configuration... }
[83] button "Copy code to clipboard"
To learn more about CPU time and limits,
[84] link "review the Workers documentation" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
.
## Wall time limits by invocation type
[85] link "" -> /queues/platform/limits/#wall-time-limits-by-invocation-type
Wall time (also called wall-clock time) is the total elapsed time from the start to end of an invocation, including time spent waiting on network requests, I/O, and other asynchronous operations. This is distinct from
[86] link "CPU time" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
, which only measures time the CPU spends actively executing your code.
The following table summarizes the wall time limits for different types of Worker invocations across the developer platform:
Invocation type
Wall time limit
Details
Incoming HTTP request
Unlimited
No hard limit while the client remains connected. Workers requests are subject to the
[87] link "grace period for runtime updates" -> /workers/platform/limits/#runtime-updates
. A Worker that is still streaming a response body remains active.
[88] link "waitUntil()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/context/#waituntil
extends execution for up to 30 seconds after the response or disconnect.
[89] link "Cron Triggers" -> /workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
15 minutes
Scheduled Workers have a maximum wall time of 15 minutes per invocation.
[90] link "Queue consumers" -> /queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer
15 minutes
Each consumer invocation has a maximum wall time of 15 minutes.
[91] link "Durable Object alarm handlers" -> /durable-objects/api/alarms/
15 minutes
Alarm handler invocations have a maximum wall time of 15 minutes.
[92] link "Durable Objects" -> /durable-objects/
(RPC / HTTP)
Unlimited
No hard limit while the caller stays connected to the Durable Object. Durable Objects remain active while a request, RPC call, response stream, WebSocket, or pending I/O is in flight.
[93] link "Workflows" -> /workflows/
(per step)
Unlimited
Each step can run for an unlimited wall time. Individual steps are subject to the configured
[94] link "CPU time limit" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
.

## CPU time
[528] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
CPU time measures how long the CPU spends executing your Worker code. Waiting on network requests (such as fetch() calls, KV reads, or database queries) does not count toward CPU time.
Limit
Workers Free
Workers Paid
CPU time per HTTP request
10 ms
5 min (default: 30 seconds)
CPU time per Cron Trigger
10 ms
30 seconds (< 1 hour interval) 15 min (>= 1 hour interval)
Most Workers consume very little CPU time. The average Worker uses approximately 2.2 ms per request. Heavier workloads that handle authentication, server-side rendering, or parse large payloads typically use 10-20 ms.
Each
[529] link "isolate" -> /workers/reference/how-workers-works/#isolates
has some built-in flexibility to allow for cases where your Worker infrequently runs over the configured limit. If your Worker starts hitting the limit consistently, its execution will be terminated according to the limit configured.
#### Error: exceeded CPU time limit
[530] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#exceeded-cpu
When a Worker exceeds its CPU time limit, Cloudflare returns
[531] link "Error 1102" -> /support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-1xxx-errors/error-1102/#error-1102-worker-exceeded-resource-limits
to the client with the message Worker exceeded resource limits . In the dashboard, this appears as Exceeded CPU Time Limits under Metrics > Errors > Invocation Statuses . In analytics and Logpush, the invocation outcome is exceededCpu .
To resolve a CPU time limit error:
Increase the CPU time limit — On the Workers Paid plan, you can raise the limit from the default 30 seconds up to 5 minutes (300,000 ms). Set this in your Wrangler configuration or in the dashboard.
Optimize your code — Use
[532] link "CPU profiling with DevTools" -> /workers/observability/dev-tools/cpu-usage/
to identify CPU-intensive sections of your code.
Offload work — Move expensive computation to
[533] link "Durable Objects" -> /durable-objects/
or process data in smaller chunks across multiple requests.
#### Increasing the CPU time limit

On the Workers Paid plan, you can increase the maximum CPU time from the default 30 seconds to 5 minutes (300,000 ms).

There is no hard limit on duration for HTTP-triggered Workers. As long as the client remains connected, the Worker can continue processing, making subrequests, and streaming a response body. When the client disconnects or the response is complete, tasks associated with that request may be canceled. Use
[559] link "ctx.waitUntil()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/context/#waituntil
to perform work after returning a response. waitUntil() can extend execution for up to 30 seconds after the response is sent or the client disconnects.
### Runtime updates
[560] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#runtime-updates
Cloudflare regularly updates the Workers runtime. During routine updates, processes running the previous version of the Workers runtime give existing Workers requests and connections up to 20 minutes to finish. This includes streaming HTTP responses and WebSocket connections.
Once the updated version of the Workers runtime is ready, it handles new incoming HTTP requests. Processes running the previous version stop accepting these requests and drain existing work during their grace period.
The grace period applies to each process running the previous version, not to each request. When it ends, that process terminates its remaining requests and connections.
Crashes, resource pressure, and shutdowns can interrupt work earlier. Design long-running applications to handle disconnections and safely retry interrupted work.

## Simultaneous open connections
[575] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#simultaneous-open-connections
Each Worker invocation can have up to six connections simultaneously waiting for response headers. The following API calls count toward this limit while the initial connection is being established and the server has not yet responded:
fetch() method of the
[576] link "Fetch API" -> /workers/runtime-apis/fetch/
get() , put() , list() , and delete() methods of
[577] link "Workers KV namespace objects" -> /kv/api/
put() , match() , and delete() methods of
[578] link "Cache objects" -> /workers/runtime-apis/cache/
list() , get() , put() , delete() , and head() methods of
[579] link "R2" -> /r2/
send() and sendBatch() methods of
[580] link "Queues" -> /queues/
Opening a TCP socket using the
[581] link "connect()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/
API
Outbound WebSocket connections also count toward this limit.
Once response headers arrive for a connection, it no longer counts toward the six-connection limit. This means a Worker can have many connections open simultaneously, as long as no more than six are in the initial "waiting for headers" phase at the same time. If a seventh connection is attempted while six are already waiting for headers, it is queued until one of the existing connections receives its response headers.
If you use fetch() but do not need the response body, calling response.body.cancel() is still good practice to free memory:
[582] tab "JavaScript"
[583] tab "TypeScript"
src/index.js
js
const response = await fetch (url); // Only read the response body for successful responses if (response.status <= 299 ) { // Call response.json(), response.text() or otherwise process the body } else { // Explicitly cancel it response.body. cancel (); }
[584] button "Copy code to clipboard"
Note
The runtime measures simultaneous open connections from the top-level request. Workers triggered via
[585] link "Service bindings" -> /workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/
share the same connection limit.

## Worker startup time
[595] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#worker-startup-time
Limit
Value
Startup time
1 second
A Worker must parse and execute its global scope (top-level code outside of handlers) within 1 second. Larger bundles and expensive initialization code in global scope increase startup time.
When the platform rejects a deployment because the Worker exceeds the startup time limit, the validation returns the error Script startup exceeded CPU time limit (error code 10021 ). Wrangler automatically generates a CPU profile that you can import into Chrome DevTools or open in VS Code. Refer to
[596] link "wrangler check startup" -> /workers/wrangler/commands/workers/#startup
for more details.
To measure startup time, run npx wrangler@latest deploy or npx wrangler@latest versions upload . Wrangler reports startup_time_ms in the output.
To reduce startup time, avoid expensive work in global scope. Move initialization logic into your handler or to build time. For example, generating or consuming a large schema at the top level is a common cause of exceeding this limit.

## CPU time
[528] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
CPU time measures how long the CPU spends executing your Worker code. Waiting on network requests (such as fetch() calls, KV reads, or database queries) does not count toward CPU time.
Limit
Workers Free
Workers Paid
CPU time per HTTP request
10 ms
5 min (default: 30 seconds)
CPU time per Cron Trigger
10 ms
30 seconds (< 1 hour interval) 15 min (>= 1 hour interval)
Most Workers consume very little CPU time. The average Worker uses approximately 2.2 ms per request. Heavier workloads that handle authentication, server-side rendering, or parse large payloads typically use 10-20 ms.
Each
[529] link "isolate" -> /workers/reference/how-workers-works/#isolates
has some built-in flexibility to allow for cases where your Worker infrequently runs over the configured limit. If your Worker starts hitting the limit consistently, its execution will be terminated according to the limit configured.
#### Error: exceeded CPU time limit
[530] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#exceeded-cpu
When a Worker exceeds its CPU time limit, Cloudflare returns
[531] link "Error 1102" -> /support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-1xxx-errors/error-1102/#error-1102-worker-exceeded-resource-limits
to the client with the message Worker exceeded resource limits . In the dashboard, this appears as Exceeded CPU Time Limits under Metrics > Errors > Invocation Statuses . In analytics and Logpush, the invocation outcome is exceededCpu .
To resolve a CPU time limit error:
Increase the CPU time limit — On the Workers Paid plan, you can raise the limit from the default 30 seconds up to 5 minutes (300,000 ms). Set this in your Wrangler configuration or in the dashboard.
Optimize your code — Use
[532] link "CPU profiling with DevTools" -> /workers/observability/dev-tools/cpu-usage/
to identify CPU-intensive sections of your code.
Offload work — Move expensive computation to
[533] link "Durable Objects" -> /durable-objects/
or process data in smaller chunks across multiple requests.
#### Increasing the CPU time limit
[534] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#increasing-the-cpu-time-limit
On the Workers Paid plan, you can increase the maximum CPU time from the default 30 seconds to 5 minutes (300,000 ms).

{ // ...rest of your configuration... "limits" : { "cpu_ms" : 300000 , // default is 30000 (30 seconds) }, // ...rest of your configuration... }

There is no hard limit on duration for HTTP-triggered Workers. As long as the client remains connected, the Worker can continue processing, making subrequests, and streaming a response body. When the client disconnects or the response is complete, tasks associated with that request may be canceled. Use
[559] link "ctx.waitUntil()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/context/#waituntil

### Runtime updates
[560] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#runtime-updates
Cloudflare regularly updates the Workers runtime. During routine updates, processes running the previous version of the Workers runtime give existing Workers requests and connections up to 20 minutes to finish. This includes streaming HTTP responses and WebSocket connections.
Once the updated version of the Workers runtime is ready, it handles new incoming HTTP requests. Processes running the previous version stop accepting these requests and drain existing work during their grace period.
The grace period applies to each process running the previous version, not to each request. When it ends, that process terminates its remaining requests and connections.
Crashes, resource pressure, and shutdowns can interrupt work earlier. Design long-running applications to handle disconnections and safely retry interrupted work.

## Simultaneous open connections
[575] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#simultaneous-open-connections
Each Worker invocation can have up to six connections simultaneously waiting for response headers. The following API calls count toward this limit while the initial connection is being established and the server has not yet responded:
fetch() method of the
[576] link "Fetch API" -> /workers/runtime-apis/fetch/
get() , put() , list() , and delete() methods of
[577] link "Workers KV namespace objects" -> /kv/api/
put() , match() , and delete() methods of
[578] link "Cache objects" -> /workers/runtime-apis/cache/
list() , get() , put() , delete() , and head() methods of
[579] link "R2" -> /r2/
send() and sendBatch() methods of
[580] link "Queues" -> /queues/
Opening a TCP socket using the
[581] link "connect()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/
API
Outbound WebSocket connections also count toward this limit.
Once response headers arrive for a connection, it no longer counts toward the six-connection limit. This means a Worker can have many connections open simultaneously, as long as no more than six are in the initial "waiting for headers" phase at the same time. If a seventh connection is attempted while six are already waiting for headers, it is queued until one of the existing connections receives its response headers.
If you use fetch() but do not need the response body, calling response.body.cancel() is still good practice to free memory:
[582] tab "JavaScript"
[583] tab "TypeScript"
src/index.js
js
const response = await fetch (url); // Only read the response body for successful responses if (response.status <= 299 ) { // Call response.json(), response.text() or otherwise process the body } else { // Explicitly cancel it response.body. cancel (); }

Note
The runtime measures simultaneous open connections from the top-level request. Workers triggered via
[585] link "Service bindings" -> /workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/
share the same connection limit.

[595] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#worker-startup-time
Limit
Value
Startup time

A Worker must parse and execute its global scope (top-level code outside of handlers) within 1 second. Larger bundles and expensive initialization code in global scope increase startup time.
When the platform rejects a deployment because the Worker exceeds the startup time limit, the validation returns the error Script startup exceeded CPU time limit (error code 10021 ). Wrangler automatically generates a CPU profile that you can import into Chrome DevTools or open in VS Code. Refer to

To measure startup time, run npx wrangler@latest deploy or npx wrangler@latest versions upload . Wrangler reports startup_time_ms in the output.
To reduce startup time, avoid expensive work in global scope. Move initialization logic into your handler or to build time. For example, generating or consuming a large schema at the top level is a common cause of exceeding this limit.

## CPU time
[528] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#cpu-time
CPU time measures how long the CPU spends executing your Worker code. Waiting on network requests (such as fetch() calls, KV reads, or database queries) does not count toward CPU time.
Limit
Workers Free
Workers Paid
CPU time per HTTP request
10 ms
5 min (default: 30 seconds)
CPU time per Cron Trigger
10 ms
30 seconds (< 1 hour interval) 15 min (>= 1 hour interval)
Most Workers consume very little CPU time. The average Worker uses approximately 2.2 ms per request. Heavier workloads that handle authentication, server-side rendering, or parse large payloads typically use 10-20 ms.
Each
[529] link "isolate" -> /workers/reference/how-workers-works/#isolates
has some built-in flexibility to allow for cases where your Worker infrequently runs over the configured limit. If your Worker starts hitting the limit consistently, its execution will be terminated according to the limit configured.
#### Error: exceeded CPU time limit
[530] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#exceeded-cpu
When a Worker exceeds its CPU time limit, Cloudflare returns
[531] link "Error 1102" -> /support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-1xxx-errors/error-1102/#error-1102-worker-exceeded-resource-limits
to the client with the message Worker exceeded resource limits . In the dashboard, this appears as Exceeded CPU Time Limits under Metrics > Errors > Invocation Statuses . In analytics and Logpush, the invocation outcome is exceededCpu .
To resolve a CPU time limit error:
Increase the CPU time limit — On the Workers Paid plan, you can raise the limit from the default 30 seconds up to 5 minutes (300,000 ms). Set this in your Wrangler configuration or in the dashboard.
Optimize your code — Use
[532] link "CPU profiling with DevTools" -> /workers/observability/dev-tools/cpu-usage/
to identify CPU-intensive sections of your code.
Offload work — Move expensive computation to
[533] link "Durable Objects" -> /durable-objects/
or process data in smaller chunks across multiple requests.
#### Increasing the CPU time limit
[534] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#increasing-the-cpu-time-limit
On the Workers Paid plan, you can increase the maximum CPU time from the default 30 seconds to 5 minutes (300,000 ms).
[535] tab "wrangler.jsonc"

{ // ...rest of your configuration... "limits" : { "cpu_ms" : 300000 , // default is 30000 (30 seconds) }, // ...rest of your configuration... }

You can also change this in the dashboard: go to Workers & Pages > select your Worker > Settings > adjust the CPU time limit.

## Simultaneous open connections
[575] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#simultaneous-open-connections
Each Worker invocation can have up to six connections simultaneously waiting for response headers. The following API calls count toward this limit while the initial connection is being established and the server has not yet responded:
fetch() method of the
[576] link "Fetch API" -> /workers/runtime-apis/fetch/
get() , put() , list() , and delete() methods of
[577] link "Workers KV namespace objects" -> /kv/api/
put() , match() , and delete() methods of
[578] link "Cache objects" -> /workers/runtime-apis/cache/
list() , get() , put() , delete() , and head() methods of
[579] link "R2" -> /r2/
send() and sendBatch() methods of
[580] link "Queues" -> /queues/
Opening a TCP socket using the
[581] link "connect()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/
API
Outbound WebSocket connections also count toward this limit.
Once response headers arrive for a connection, it no longer counts toward the six-connection limit. This means a Worker can have many connections open simultaneously, as long as no more than six are in the initial "waiting for headers" phase at the same time. If a seventh connection is attempted while six are already waiting for headers, it is queued until one of the existing connections receives its response headers.
If you use fetch() but do not need the response body, calling response.body.cancel() is still good practice to free memory:
[582] tab "JavaScript"

src/index.js
js
const response = await fetch (url); // Only read the response body for successful responses if (response.status <= 299 ) { // Call response.json(), response.text() or otherwise process the body } else { // Explicitly cancel it response.body. cancel (); }

Note
The runtime measures simultaneous open connections from the top-level request. Workers triggered via
[585] link "Service bindings" -> /workers/runtime-apis/bindings/service-bindings/
share the same connection limit.

## Worker startup time
[595] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#worker-startup-time
Limit
Value
Startup time
1 second
A Worker must parse and execute its global scope (top-level code outside of handlers) within 1 second. Larger bundles and expensive initialization code in global scope increase startup time.
When the platform rejects a deployment because the Worker exceeds the startup time limit, the validation returns the error Script startup exceeded CPU time limit (error code 10021 ). Wrangler automatically generates a CPU profile that you can import into Chrome DevTools or open in VS Code. Refer to
[596] link "wrangler check startup" -> /workers/wrangler/commands/workers/#startup
for more details.
To measure startup time, run npx wrangler@latest deploy or npx wrangler@latest versions upload . Wrangler reports startup_time_ms in the output.
To reduce startup time, avoid expensive work in global scope. Move initialization logic into your handler or to build time. For example, generating or consuming a large schema at the top level is a common cause of exceeding this limit.

There is no hard limit on duration for HTTP-triggered Workers. As long as the client remains connected, the Worker can continue processing, making subrequests, and streaming a response body. When the client disconnects or the response is complete, tasks associated with that request may be canceled. Use
[559] link "ctx.waitUntil()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/context/#waituntil

### Runtime updates
[560] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#runtime-updates
Cloudflare regularly updates the Workers runtime. During routine updates, processes running the previous version of the Workers runtime give existing Workers requests and connections up to 20 minutes to finish. This includes streaming HTTP responses and WebSocket connections.
Once the updated version of the Workers runtime is ready, it handles new incoming HTTP requests. Processes running the previous version stop accepting these requests and drain existing work during their grace period.
The grace period applies to each process running the previous version, not to each request. When it ends, that process terminates its remaining requests and connections.
Crashes, resource pressure, and shutdowns can interrupt work earlier. Design long-running applications to handle disconnections and safely retry interrupted work.

[561] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#daily-requests

Accounts on the Workers Free plan have a daily request limit of 100,000 requests, resetting at midnight UTC. When a Worker exceeds this limit, Cloudflare returns Error 1027 .

[575] link "" -> /workers/platform/limits/#simultaneous-open-connections
Each Worker invocation can have up to six connections simultaneously waiting for response headers. The following API calls count toward this limit while the initial connection is being established and the server has not yet responded:
fetch() method of the
[576] link "Fetch API" -> /workers/runtime-apis/fetch/
get() , put() , list() , and delete() methods of
[577] link "Workers KV namespace objects" -> /kv/api/
put() , match() , and delete() methods of
[578] link "Cache objects" -> /workers/runtime-apis/cache/
list() , get() , put() , delete() , and head() methods of
[579] link "R2" -> /r2/
send() and sendBatch() methods of
[580] link "Queues" -> /queues/
Opening a TCP socket using the
[581] link "connect()" -> /workers/runtime-apis/tcp-sockets/
API

This means a Worker can have many connections open simultaneously, as long as no more than six are in the initial "waiting for headers" phase at the same time. If a seventh connection is attempted while six are already waiting for headers, it is queued until one of the existing connections receives its response headers.

Wall time (also called wall-clock time) is the total elapsed time from the start to end of an invocation, including time spent waiting on network requests, I/O, and other asynchronous operations. This is distinct from

(RPC / HTTP)

Notion API
# Connections and tokens
Compare personal access tokens, internal connections, OAuth integrations, and public integrations for your Notion app or automation.
[60] button "Copy page"
[61] button "More actions"
Choose a personal access token, internal connection, OAuth integration, or public integration based on who will use your app and how it needs to access Notion.
## ​Choose the right option
[62] link "Automate your own workUse a personal access token for scripts, tools, and Workers that run with your Notion permissions."
[63] link "Build a shared workspace toolUse an internal connection for tools your team shares, with access granted to the connection independently of any one person."
[64] link "Build an app for your workspacesUse an OAuth integration for internal tools where each person authorizes their own access. Your app acts on behalf of the user who connects it."
[65] link "Build an app for any workspaceUse a public integration so users in any workspace can authorize your app through OAuth. You can also apply to list it on the Marketplace."
## ​Compare the options
OAuth integrations and public integrations use the same OAuth authorization flow. Here, OAuth integrations are limited to selected workspaces, while public integrations are available to any workspace.

## ​Shared concepts
### ​Capabilities
[66] link "Capabilities" -> /reference/capabilities
determine which operations a connection or token can perform, such as reading pages, updating databases, or adding comments. Choose the capabilities your app needs.
### ​Content access
Capabilities and content access work together: permission to update pages does not grant access to every page. A personal access token uses your existing permissions. An internal connection needs content access granted to it. For OAuth integrations and public integrations, each user grants access during authorization. To share content:
Internal connections: Add the page or database in the Developer portal’s Content access tab, or open it in Notion and use Add connections . See
[67] link "Granting page access" -> /guides/connections-and-tokens/internal-connections#granting-page-access
for the steps.
OAuth integrations and public integrations: Each user selects pages in the OAuth page picker when authorizing the app. Selecting a parent page also grants access to its child pages. See
[68] link "Selecting pages during authorization" -> /guides/authorization/overview#select-pages-to-share
.
Personal access tokens: No separate sharing step is needed. The token uses its creator’s existing permissions, limited by its capabilities.
### ​Webhooks
Internal connections, OAuth integrations, and public integrations can subscribe to
[69] link "webhooks" -> /reference/webhooks
to respond to changes such as page updates and new comments. Use these when your app needs to react to changes without repeatedly checking the API.
## ​Getting started
Try the
[70] link "Quickstart" -> /guides/notion-api/quick-start
to create a page with a personal access token. For setup instructions and permissions, choose one of the guides above.
See
[71] link "Authorization" -> /guides/authorization/overview
for token authentication and OAuth flows, and
[72] link "API credential security" -> /guides/authorization/credential-security
for storing and protecting credentials.

# Introduction
Find the base URL, headers, and data formats for Notion API requests.
[65] button "Copy page"
[66] button "More actions"
Send requests over HTTPS to https://api.notion.com . To make your first request, follow the
[67] link "API quickstart" -> /guides/notion-api/quick-start

## ​Conventions
For requests to pages, databases, and other workspace resources, send an Authorization: Bearer header with your token and a
[68] link "Notion-Version header" -> /reference/versioning
. The
[69] link "authentication reference" -> /reference/authentication

Most endpoints use JSON. Set Content-Type: application/json when you send a JSON body.
[70] link "Sending a file" -> /reference/upload-file
uses multipart form data instead.
### ​JSON conventions
The object field identifies a resource, such as a page or user .
You can send page and database IDs with or without dashes.
Property names use snake_case .
Dates and timestamps use ISO 8601, such as 2026-03-11 or 2026-03-11T09:30:00.000Z .
To clear a
[71] link "URL page property" -> /reference/page-property-values#url
, send null .

[72] link "JavaScript SDK" -> https://github.com/makenotion/notion-sdk-js
, curl, or any client that can send HTTPS requests. Each endpoint reference lists its parameters and response fields. See
[73] link "status codes" -> /reference/status-codes
to interpret an error response.

Notion API
# Pagination
Read lists of results with cursor-based pagination in the Notion API.
[65] button "Copy page"
[66] button "More actions"
A paginated endpoint returns part of a list at a time. Read has_more to tell whether another page is available. A page can contain fewer items than you requested even when more remain.
## ​Requests
Parameter
Meaning
start_cursor
Omit it on the first request. For the next page, pass the previous response’s next_cursor unchanged.
page_size
The maximum number of items to return in one response. Most list endpoints default to 100 and accept values from 1 to 100.
For GET requests, pass these parameters in the query string. For
[67] link "search" -> /reference/post-search
and
[68] link "data source queries" -> /reference/query-a-data-source
, pass them in the POST body. Keep the same filters and sort order between requests.
## ​Responses
Field
Meaning
results
The items on this page of a standard list response.
has_more
true if another page of results is available.
next_cursor
The cursor for the next page, or null at the end of a standard list.
A standard list has object: "list" . Its type identifies the kind of result. For
[69] link "paginated page properties" -> /reference/property-item-object#paginated-values
, the response also includes information about the property.
[70] link "List data source templates" -> /reference/list-data-source-templates
returns items in templates . When you
[71] link "create a view query" -> /reference/create-view-query
, use its query_id with
[72] link "Get view query results" -> /reference/get-view-query-results
to read subsequent pages.
## ​Paginated endpoints
The endpoint reference gives the shape of each result. Common examples include
[73] link "block children" -> /reference/get-block-children
,
[74] link "users" -> /reference/get-users
,
[75] link "comments" -> /reference/list-comments
,
[76] link "file uploads" -> /reference/list-file-uploads
,
[77] link "custom emojis" -> /reference/list-custom-emojis
, and
[78] link "views" -> /reference/list-views
.
## ​Example
Set NOTION_API_KEY to your token and NOTION_BLOCK_ID to a page or block your token can read. The curl request requests up to two children. The JavaScript SDK example follows each cursor and prints one child ID at a time.
[79] tab "curl"
[80] tab "JavaScript SDK"
[81] button "Report incorrect code"
[82] button "Copy the contents from the code block"
[83] button "Ask Assistant"
curl --get "https://api.notion.com/v1/blocks/ $NOTION_BLOCK_ID /children" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $NOTION_API_KEY " \ -H "Notion-Version: 2026-03-11" \ --data-urlencode "page_size=2"
For a large data source, a single query can reach its result limit even when has_more is false. See
[84] link "Query large data sources" -> /guides/data-apis/query-large-data-sources
to detect the limit and read the remaining rows.

Notion API
# Connections and tokens
Compare personal access tokens, internal connections, OAuth integrations, and public integrations for your Notion app or automation.
[60] button "Copy page"
[61] button "More actions"
Choose a personal access token, internal connection, OAuth integration, or public integration based on who will use your app and how it needs to access Notion.
## ​Choose the right option
[62] link "Automate your own workUse a personal access token for scripts, tools, and Workers that run with your Notion permissions."
[63] link "Build a shared workspace toolUse an internal connection for tools your team shares, with access granted to the connection independently of any one person."
[64] link "Build an app for your workspacesUse an OAuth integration for internal tools where each person authorizes their own access. Your app acts on behalf of the user who connects it."
[65] link "Build an app for any workspaceUse a public integration so users in any workspace can authorize your app through OAuth. You can also apply to list it on the Marketplace."
## ​Compare the options
OAuth integrations and public integrations use the same OAuth authorization flow. Here, OAuth integrations are limited to selected workspaces, while public integrations are available to any workspace.
Personal access token
Internal connection
OAuth integration
Public integration
Workspace scope

One workspace.
Workspaces you select when creating the integration.

Whose access does it use?
Yours.

Each user’s separately authorized access.
Content access
Uses your existing page permissions.
Uses permissions granted to the connection.

Authentication

Marketplace listing

## ​Shared concepts
### ​Capabilities
[66] link "Capabilities" -> /reference/capabilities
determine which operations a connection or token can perform, such as reading pages, updating databases, or adding comments. Choose the capabilities your app needs.
### ​Content access
Capabilities and content access work together: permission to update pages does not grant access to every page. A personal access token uses your existing permissions. An internal connection needs content access granted to it. For OAuth integrations and public integrations, each user grants access during authorization. To share content:
Internal connections: Add the page or database in the Developer portal’s Content access tab, or open it in Notion and use Add connections . See
[67] link "Granting page access" -> /guides/connections-and-tokens/internal-connections#granting-page-access
for the steps.
OAuth integrations and public integrations: Each user selects pages in the OAuth page picker when authorizing the app. Selecting a parent page also grants access to its child pages. See
[68] link "Selecting pages during authorization" -> /guides/authorization/overview#select-pages-to-share
.
Personal access tokens: No separate sharing step is needed. The token uses its creator’s existing permissions, limited by its capabilities.
### ​Webhooks
Internal connections, OAuth integrations, and public integrations can subscribe to
[69] link "webhooks" -> /reference/webhooks
to respond to changes such as page updates and new comments. Use these when your app needs to react to changes without repeatedly checking the API.
## ​Getting started
Try the
[70] link "Quickstart" -> /guides/notion-api/quick-start
to create a page with a personal access token. For setup instructions and permissions, choose one of the guides above.
See
[71] link "Authorization" -> /guides/authorization/overview
for token authentication and OAuth flows, and
[72] link "API credential security" -> /guides/authorization/credential-security
for storing and protecting credentials.

Internal connections: Add the page or database in the Developer portal’s Content access tab, or open it in Notion and use Add connections . See
[67] link "Granting page access" -> /guides/connections-and-tokens/internal-connections#granting-page-access

OAuth integrations and public integrations: Each user selects pages in the OAuth page picker when authorizing the app. Selecting a parent page also grants access to its child pages. See
[68] link "Selecting pages during authorization" -> /guides/authorization/overview#select-pages-to-share
.
Personal access tokens: No separate sharing step is needed. The token uses its creator’s existing permissions, limited by its capabilities.

[69] link "webhooks" -> /reference/webhooks
to respond to changes such as page updates and new comments. Use these when your app needs to react to changes without repeatedly checking the API.

## ​Conventions
For requests to pages, databases, and other workspace resources, send an Authorization: Bearer header with your token and a
[68] link "Notion-Version header" -> /reference/versioning

[69] link "authentication reference" -> /reference/authentication

Most endpoints use JSON. Set Content-Type: application/json when you send a JSON body.

### ​JSON conventions
The object field identifies a resource, such as a page or user .
You can send page and database IDs with or without dashes.
Property names use snake_case .
Dates and timestamps use ISO 8601, such as 2026-03-11 or 2026-03-11T09:30:00.000Z .
To clear a
[71] link "URL page property" -> /reference/page-property-values#url
, send null .

Notion API
# Pagination
Read lists of results with cursor-based pagination in the Notion API.
[65] button "Copy page"
[66] button "More actions"
A paginated endpoint returns part of a list at a time. Read has_more to tell whether another page is available. A page can contain fewer items than you requested even when more remain.
## ​Requests
Parameter
Meaning
start_cursor
Omit it on the first request. For the next page, pass the previous response’s next_cursor unchanged.
page_size
The maximum number of items to return in one response. Most list endpoints default to 100 and accept values from 1 to 100.
For GET requests, pass these parameters in the query string. For
[67] link "search" -> /reference/post-search
and
[68] link "data source queries" -> /reference/query-a-data-source
, pass them in the POST body. Keep the same filters and sort order between requests.
## ​Responses
Field
Meaning
results
The items on this page of a standard list response.
has_more
true if another page of results is available.
next_cursor
The cursor for the next page, or null at the end of a standard list.
A standard list has object: "list" . Its type identifies the kind of result. For
[69] link "paginated page properties" -> /reference/property-item-object#paginated-values
, the response also includes information about the property.
[70] link "List data source templates" -> /reference/list-data-source-templates
returns items in templates . When you
[71] link "create a view query" -> /reference/create-view-query
, use its query_id with
[72] link "Get view query results" -> /reference/get-view-query-results
to read subsequent pages.
## ​Paginated endpoints
The endpoint reference gives the shape of each result. Common examples include
[73] link "block children" -> /reference/get-block-children
,
[74] link "users" -> /reference/get-users
,
[75] link "comments" -> /reference/list-comments
,
[76] link "file uploads" -> /reference/list-file-uploads
,
[77] link "custom emojis" -> /reference/list-custom-emojis
, and
[78] link "views" -> /reference/list-views
.
## ​Example
Set NOTION_API_KEY to your token and NOTION_BLOCK_ID to a page or block your token can read. The curl request requests up to two children. The JavaScript SDK example follows each cursor and prints one child ID at a time.
[79] tab "curl"
[80] tab "JavaScript SDK"
[81] button "Report incorrect code"
[82] button "Copy the contents from the code block"
[83] button "Ask Assistant"

For a large data source, a single query can reach its result limit even when has_more is false. See
[84] link "Query large data sources" -> /guides/data-apis/query-large-data-sources
