calls.result: Page: The checklist · Website Spec (https://specification.website/checklist/) [1] link "Skip to main content" -> /checklist/#main [2] link "Website SpecWhat a good website does." -> / [3] link "All topics" -> /spec/ [4] link "Checklist" -> /checklist/ [5] link "Changelog" -> /changelog/ [6] link "MCP" -> /mcp/ [7] link "About" -> /about/ [8] link "Contribute" -> /contribute/ [9] button "Open search (Command-K)" [10] switch "Switch to light theme" [11] link "Home" -> / / Checklist # The checklist Every spec item, flat and tickable. Use as a self-audit. Print-friendly. Prefer to track it elsewhere? Grab the [12] link "Markdown version" -> /checklist.md — GitHub-style - [ ] task list, ready to paste into an issue or a note. [13] link "Foundations" -> /checklist/#foundations [14] link "SEO" -> /checklist/#seo [15] link "Accessibility" -> /checklist/#accessibility [16] link "Security" -> /checklist/#security [17] link "Well-Known URIs" -> /checklist/#well-known [18] link "Agent Readiness" -> /checklist/#agent-readiness [19] link "Performance" -> /checklist/#performance [20] link "Privacy" -> /checklist/#privacy [21] link "Resilience" -> /checklist/#resilience [22] link "Internationalisation" -> /checklist/#i18n ## Foundations The HTML, head, and document basics every page needs. [23] input type=checkbox "Mark The HTML doctype done" value="on" [24] link "The HTML doctype" -> /spec/foundations/doctype/ Required Every HTML document must start with as its first line. This opts the browser into standards mode; without it, you get quirks mode and broken layout. [25] input type=checkbox "Mark The lang attribute on done" value="on" [26] link "The lang attribute on " -> /spec/foundations/html-lang/ Required Set a valid BCP 47 language tag on the element so screen readers, translators, search engines, and browsers know what language the page is in. [27] input type=checkbox "Mark done" value="on" [28] link "" -> /spec/foundations/meta-charset/ Required Declare UTF-8 as the document character encoding in the first 1024 bytes of the HTML, so browsers parse text correctly before they hit any non-ASCII content. [29] input type=checkbox "Mark done" value="on" [30] link "" -> /spec/foundations/meta-viewport/ Required Tell mobile browsers to render the page at the device's actual width instead of pretending to be a 980-pixel desktop. One line, and never disable user scaling. [31] input type=checkbox "Mark The element done" value="on" [32] link "The <title> element" -> /spec/foundations/title/ Required Every HTML document must have exactly one non-empty <title> element inside <head>. It names the page for browsers, search engines, screen readers, social previews, and AI agents. It is not the same thing as the page's <h1>. [33] input type=checkbox "Mark <meta name="description"> done" value="on" [34] link "<meta name="description">" -> /spec/foundations/meta-description/ Recommended A short, unique summary of the page used by search engines and social platforms as a snippet. Google may rewrite it, but a good one is rewritten less often. [35] input type=checkbox "Mark Canonical URL (rel="canonical") done" value="on" [36] link "Canonical URL (rel="canonical")" -> /spec/foundations/canonical-url/ Recommended Declare the preferred URL for a page so search engines and crawlers consolidate ranking signals on one address, even when several URLs serve the same content. [37] input type=checkbox "Mark Favicons and app icons done" value="on" [38] link "Favicons and app icons" -> /spec/foundations/favicons/ Recommended Ship an SVG favicon, an ICO fallback at /favicon.ico, an apple-touch-icon, and a maskable PWA icon. Five files cover every browser and home-screen surface. [39] input type=checkbox "Mark <meta name="theme-color"> done" value="on" [40] link "<meta name="theme-color">" -> /spec/foundations/theme-color/ Recommended Tints the browser chrome and OS surfaces to match your brand. Use the media attribute to ship one colour for light mode and another for dark mode. [41] input type=checkbox "Mark <meta name="color-scheme"> done" value="on" [42] link "<meta name="color-scheme">" -> /spec/foundations/color-scheme/ Recommended Tells the browser which colour schemes your page is designed for. Prevents the white flash that dark-mode users see before your CSS loads, and lets the browser style scrollbars, form controls, and the page background to match. [43] input type=checkbox "Mark Open Graph protocol done" value="on" [44] link "Open Graph protocol" -> /spec/foundations/open-graph/ Recommended Open Graph tags control how pages look when shared on social platforms and chat apps. Set og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url, and og:type on every page. [45] input type=checkbox "Mark Feed discovery with rel="alternate" done" value="on" [46] link "Feed discovery with rel="alternate"" -> /spec/foundations/feed-discovery/ Recommended If your site publishes a feed — RSS, Atom, or JSON Feed — announce it in <head> with <link rel="alternate">. Feed readers, agents, and browsers discover it without guessing the URL. [47] input type=checkbox "Mark Feed content hygiene done" value="on" [48] link "Feed content hygiene" -> /spec/foundations/feed-hygiene/ Recommended If you publish a feed, ship it well-formed. Identify the feed inside itself with atom:link rel="self", give every item a stable guid, declare an update cadence with the Syndication module, and validate before deploy. [49] input type=checkbox "Mark Popover API done" value="on" [50] link "Popover API" -> /spec/foundations/popover-api/ Recommended Replace ARIA-puzzled JavaScript modals, menus, and tooltips with a native top-layer primitive that the browser opens, closes, and accessibility-wires for you. [51] input type=checkbox "Mark WebSub — push notification for feeds done" value="on" [52] link "WebSub — push notification for feeds" -> /spec/foundations/websub/ Optional If you publish a feed, advertise a WebSub hub with rel="hub" and rel="self" so subscribers are pushed each update instead of polling for it. Cuts latency to seconds and removes most of the crawl traffic your feed attracts. [53] input type=checkbox "Mark CSS anchor positioning done" value="on" [54] link "CSS anchor positioning" -> /spec/foundations/anchor-positioning/ Recommended Tether tooltips, menus, and popovers to the element that triggers them with pure CSS — no JavaScript positioning library, and it works across overflow and stacking boundaries. [55] input type=checkbox "Mark Balanced text wrapping done" value="on" [56] link "Balanced text wrapping" -> /spec/foundations/text-wrap/ Recommended Let the browser break headings and body copy intelligently with text-wrap: balance and pretty — no orphaned words, no manual line breaks, no layout shift. [57] input type=checkbox "Mark CSS container queries done" value="on" [58] link "CSS container queries" -> /spec/foundations/container-queries/ Recommended Style a component by the space it is actually given with container-type and @container — responsive design that follows the container, not the viewport — and test a container's own custom properties with style queries. [59] input type=checkbox "Mark Invoker commands done" value="on" [60] link "Invoker commands" -> /spec/foundations/invoker-commands/ Optional Wire a button to open a popover, close a dialog, or run a custom action declaratively with command and commandfor — no click handler, no ARIA plumbing. [61] input type=checkbox "Mark _for-sale DNS records done" value="on" [62] link "_for-sale DNS records" -> /spec/foundations/for-sale-dns/ Optional If a domain is genuinely for sale, say so in DNS. A TXT record at _for-sale.example.com advertises it to brokers and availability services without taking the site down or parking it. ## SEO Search visibility — robots.txt, sitemaps, canonicals, structured data. [63] input type=checkbox "Mark robots.txt done" value="on" [64] link "robots.txt" -> /spec/seo/robots-txt/ Recommended A plain-text file at the site root that tells crawlers which paths they may or may not fetch. Standardised in RFC 9309 and supported by every major search engine. [65] input type=checkbox "Mark XML sitemaps done" value="on" [66] link "XML sitemaps" -> /spec/seo/xml-sitemaps/ Recommended An XML file listing the canonical URLs of a site, with optional metadata about when each was last changed. The fastest way to tell a search engine what exists. [67] input type=checkbox "Mark Sitemap index files done" value="on" [68] link "Sitemap index files" -> /spec/seo/sitemap-index/ Recommended A sitemap of sitemaps. Used when a site has more than 50,000 URLs or wants to split sitemaps by content type for cleaner reporting. [69] input type=checkbox "Mark Image and video sitemap extensions done" value="on" [70] link "Image and video sitemap extensions" -> /spec/seo/image-sitemaps/ Optional Optional XML extensions that add image and video metadata to sitemap entries. Useful when media is loaded by JavaScript or hosted on a CDN that crawlers cannot reach by following links. [71] input type=checkbox "Mark URL structure done" value="on" [72] link "URL structure" -> /spec/seo/url-structure/ Recommended URLs are the most stable identifier on the web. Keep them lowercase, hyphenated, descriptive, and shallow. Treat them as a public API for your content. [73] input type=checkbox "Mark Redirects (301/302/308) done" value="on" [74] link "Redirects (301/302/308)" -> /spec/seo/redirects/ Required HTTP redirects send a client from one URL to another. Use 301 or 308 for permanent moves, 302 or 307 for temporary ones, and never chain more than necessary. [75] input type=checkbox "Mark Server-side rendering done" value="on" [76] link "Server-side rendering" -> /spec/seo/server-side-rendering/ Recommended Crawlers, social scrapers, and AI agents index the HTML your server returns. Render your primary content and metadata server-side — via SSR, static generation, or prerendering — so it is in the initial response, not assembled later by client-side JavaScript. [77] input type=checkbox "Mark Soft 404s done" value="on" [78] link "Soft 404s" -> /spec/seo/soft-404/ Avoid A page that looks like a 'not found' message to a user but returns 200 OK to a crawler. Search engines treat soft 404s as a quality problem and often refuse to index them. [79] input type=checkbox "Mark Meta robots and X-Robots-Tag done" value="on" [80] link "Meta robots and X-Robots-Tag" -> /spec/seo/meta-robots/ Required Every page must have an explicit, correct indexing policy — either implicit (default index, follow) on public pages, or an explicit noindex / X-Robots-Tag on staging, admin, thin, or private content. Get this wrong and you either disappear from search or expose what you didn't mean to. [81] input type=checkbox "Mark Heading hierarchy done" value="on" [82] link "Heading hierarchy" -> /spec/seo/heading-hierarchy/ Required Headings describe the sections of a page. They must form a nested outline, never be used for visual styling alone, and never skip levels. [83] input type=checkbox "Mark Internal linking done" value="on" [84] link "Internal linking" -> /spec/seo/internal-linking/ Recommended Links from one page on a site to another. The strongest signal you control for telling crawlers and AI agents what a page is about and how important it is. [85] input type=checkbox "Mark Structured data (JSON-LD) done" value="on" [86] link "Structured data (JSON-LD)" -> /spec/seo/structured-data/ Recommended Machine-readable annotations that describe the content of a page using the schema.org vocabulary. JSON-LD is the format search engines and AI agents expect. [87] input type=checkbox "Mark Breadcrumbs done" value="on" [88] link "Breadcrumbs" -> /spec/seo/breadcrumbs/ Recommended A short trail showing the page's position in the site hierarchy. Visible in the UI for users, marked up as BreadcrumbList JSON-LD for search engines. [89] input type=checkbox "Mark IndexNow done" value="on" [90] link "IndexNow" -> /spec/seo/indexnow/ Optional An open protocol for telling participating search engines that a URL has changed. One HTTP request pushes Bing, Yandex, Naver, and Seznam to recrawl — Google does not participate. ## Accessibility WCAG-aligned rules so people of all abilities can use the site. [91] input type=checkbox "Mark Colour contrast done" value="on" [92] link "Colour contrast" -> /spec/accessibility/color-contrast/ Required Text and meaningful non-text elements must have enough contrast against their background so people with low vision and people in harsh light can read them. [93] input type=checkbox "Mark Automatic contrasting colour done" value="on" [94] link "Automatic contrasting colour" -> /spec/accessibility/contrast-color/ Optional Let the browser pick a legible black or white foreground for a dynamic background with the CSS contrast-color() function, instead of hard-coding colour pairs or computing luminance in JavaScript. [95] input type=checkbox "Mark Forced colours mode done" value="on" [96] link "Forced colours mode" -> /spec/accessibility/forced-colors/ Recommended Respect forced colours mode (Windows High Contrast and similar). The `forced-colors` media feature lets you repair UI the user's palette would otherwise flatten — without overriding their choice. [97] input type=checkbox "Mark Image alt text done" value="on" [98] link "Image alt text" -> /spec/accessibility/image-alt-text/ Required Every <img> element must have an alt attribute. The value describes the image's purpose to screen readers, search engines, and anyone whose image fails to load. [99] input type=checkbox "Mark Form labels done" value="on" [100] link "Form labels" -> /spec/accessibility/form-labels/ Required Every form control needs a programmatically associated label. A placeholder is not a label, and an unlabelled input is unusable for screen-reader and voice-control users. [101] input type=checkbox "Mark Keyboard navigation done" value="on" [102] link "Keyboard navigation" -> /spec/accessibility/keyboard-navigation/ Required Every interactive element on the page must be reachable and operable with a keyboard alone, in a logical order, with no traps that hold focus. [103] input type=checkbox "Mark Visible focus indicators done" value="on" [104] link "Visible focus indicators" -> /spec/accessibility/focus-indicators/ Required Whenever a control receives keyboard focus, the page must show a clear, high-contrast indicator. Removing focus outlines without a replacement is a top accessibility failure. [105] input type=checkbox "Mark Focus not obscured done" value="on" [106] link "Focus not obscured" -> /spec/accessibility/focus-not-obscured/ Recommended A focused control must not be hidden behind a sticky header, cookie banner, or chat widget. WCAG 2.2 added this as a separate criterion because a perfect focus ring is worthless if something is sitting on top of it. [107] input type=checkbox "Mark Skip links done" value="on" [108] link "Skip links" -> /spec/accessibility/skip-links/ Required A 'skip to main content' link as the first focusable element lets keyboard and screen-reader users jump past repeated navigation on every page. [109] input type=checkbox "Mark The inert attribute done" value="on" [110] link "The inert attribute" -> /spec/accessibility/inert-attribute/ Recommended When an overlay is open, the content behind it should be unreachable — not just dimmed. The inert attribute removes a subtree from tab order and the accessibility tree at once, replacing fragile focus-trap JavaScript. [111] input type=checkbox "Mark Semantic HTML and landmarks done" value="on" [112] link "Semantic HTML and landmarks" -> /spec/accessibility/semantic-html/ Required Use the right HTML element for the job. Landmarks like <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> let assistive technologies announce structure and skip between regions. [113] input type=checkbox "Mark ARIA — first rule of ARIA done" value="on" [114] link "ARIA — first rule of ARIA" -> /spec/accessibility/aria-usage/ Recommended ARIA can make custom widgets accessible, but the first rule of ARIA is don't use ARIA. Reach for a native HTML element first; add ARIA only when nothing native fits. [115] input type=checkbox "Mark Descriptive link text done" value="on" [116] link "Descriptive link text" -> /spec/accessibility/link-text/ Required Every link's text must describe where it goes. 'Click here' and 'read more' fail screen-reader users who scan a page by jumping from link to link. [117] input type=checkbox "Mark Empty links and buttons done" value="on" [118] link "Empty links and buttons" -> /spec/accessibility/empty-links-buttons/ Avoid A link or button with no accessible name is invisible to screen readers and unreachable for voice control. Icon-only controls without a label are the usual culprit. [119] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessible form errors done" value="on" [120] link "Accessible form errors" -> /spec/accessibility/form-errors/ Required When a form submission fails, errors must be identified in text, associated with the input that caused them, and announced to assistive technology. [121] input type=checkbox "Mark Status messages done" value="on" [122] link "Status messages" -> /spec/accessibility/status-messages/ Recommended When something succeeds, fails or changes without moving focus — a result count, a saved confirmation, a progress update — assistive technology has to be told. Expose it through a live region, or announce it with ariaNotify(). [123] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessible authentication done" value="on" [124] link "Accessible authentication" -> /spec/accessibility/accessible-authentication/ Recommended Let people log in without solving a puzzle, transcribing a code, or memorising anything. Don't block password managers, allow paste, and offer a method that needs no cognitive function test. [125] input type=checkbox "Mark Redundant entry done" value="on" [126] link "Redundant entry" -> /spec/accessibility/redundant-entry/ Recommended Don't make people re-type information they already gave you in the same process. Auto-populate it, or let them pick it from what they entered a step ago. [127] input type=checkbox "Mark Consistent help done" value="on" [128] link "Consistent help" -> /spec/accessibility/consistent-help/ Recommended If you offer help — a contact link, a phone number, a chat widget, an FAQ — put it in the same relative place on every page that has it. Moving it around is the failure. [129] input type=checkbox "Mark Document and parts language done" value="on" [130] link "Document and parts language" -> /spec/accessibility/document-language/ Required Set the page's primary language on <html lang> and mark any inline content in a different language with its own lang attribute, so screen readers pronounce it correctly. [131] input type=checkbox "Mark Reduced motion done" value="on" [132] link "Reduced motion" -> /spec/accessibility/reduced-motion/ Required Respect the user's `prefers-reduced-motion` setting. Decorative animation, parallax, and autoplay can trigger vestibular distress, migraines, and seizures. [133] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessibility overlays done" value="on" [134] link "Accessibility overlays" -> /spec/accessibility/accessibility-overlays/ Avoid Third-party JavaScript widgets that claim to make a site WCAG-compliant at runtime. They do not work, often harm screen-reader users, and attract lawsuits. [135] input type=checkbox "Mark Captions and transcripts done" value="on" [136] link "Captions and transcripts" -> /spec/accessibility/captions-and-transcripts/ Required Video needs synchronised captions, audio-only content needs a transcript, and visuals that carry meaning need audio description. Auto-captions alone are not enough. [137] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessible data tables done" value="on" [138] link "Accessible data tables" -> /spec/accessibility/data-tables/ Required Tabular data must use real <table> markup with a caption, header cells, and scope attributes so screen readers can announce row and column relationships. [139] input type=checkbox "Mark Touch target size done" value="on" [140] link "Touch target size" -> /spec/accessibility/touch-target-size/ Required Interactive controls must be large enough to tap or click reliably. WCAG 2.2 sets a 24×24 CSS px minimum, with 44×44 CSS px as the enhanced target. [141] input type=checkbox "Mark Dragging movements done" value="on" [142] link "Dragging movements" -> /spec/accessibility/dragging-movements/ Recommended Anything you can drag must also work with a single pointer that never drags. Sliders, sortable lists, and drag-to-pan maps each need a click or tap alternative. [143] input type=checkbox "Mark Hidden until found done" value="on" [144] link "Hidden until found" -> /spec/accessibility/hidden-until-found/ Recommended Use hidden="until-found" for collapsible content so that browser find-in-page, assistive tech, and search engines can still reach the text and auto-expand it. [145] input type=checkbox "Mark Mobile-friendly form inputs done" value="on" [146] link "Mobile-friendly form inputs" -> /spec/accessibility/mobile-form-inputs/ Recommended On a phone, the right input type, inputmode, and enterkeyhint summon the correct on-screen keyboard and a useful Enter key. Keep input text at 16px or larger so iOS Safari doesn't zoom on focus. [147] input type=checkbox "Mark Native interactive elements done" value="on" [148] link "Native interactive elements" -> /spec/accessibility/native-interactive-elements/ Recommended Prefer native HTML interactive elements — <button>, <a>, <details>/<summary>, <dialog> — over divs with click handlers. You get keyboard support, focus management, and assistive-tech semantics for free. [149] input type=checkbox "Mark CSS state and relational selectors done" value="on" [150] link "CSS state and relational selectors" -> /spec/accessibility/css-state-selectors/ Recommended Use `:has()` together with `:user-invalid`, `:user-valid`, `:placeholder-shown` and `:focus-within` to express form and component state in CSS, removing the JavaScript class-toggling pattern and the race conditions it brings. ## Security Headers, transport, and policies that keep visitors safe. [151] input type=checkbox "Mark HTTPS and TLS done" value="on" [152] link "HTTPS and TLS" -> /spec/security/https-tls/ Required Serve every page over HTTPS using TLS 1.2 or 1.3, redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS, and disable obsolete SSL and early TLS versions on every host you control. [153] input type=checkbox "Mark TLS configuration hardening done" value="on" [154] link "TLS configuration hardening" -> /spec/security/tls-configuration/ Recommended Beyond protocol versions and key exchange: TLS compression off, secure renegotiation only, no unsafe 0-RTT, Extended Main Secret on, server cipher order, SHA-2 signatures, and certificate keys of adequate size. [155] input type=checkbox "Mark HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) done" value="on" [156] link "HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)" -> /spec/security/hsts/ Required HSTS tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS for your domain. Send max-age with includeSubDomains — but skip the preload list, which its own operator now discourages. [157] input type=checkbox "Mark Mixed content and upgrade-insecure-requests done" value="on" [158] link "Mixed content and upgrade-insecure-requests" -> /spec/security/mixed-content/ Recommended An HTTPS page that loads any subresource over HTTP is mixed content. Serve every subresource over HTTPS, and send the upgrade-insecure-requests CSP directive as a safety net. [159] input type=checkbox "Mark Content Security Policy (CSP) done" value="on" [160] link "Content Security Policy (CSP)" -> /spec/security/content-security-policy/ Recommended A CSP tells browsers which sources of script, style, image, and frame content to trust. A good policy stops most XSS and data-exfiltration attacks dead. [161] input type=checkbox "Mark Reporting API (Reporting-Endpoints) done" value="on" [162] link "Reporting API (Reporting-Endpoints)" -> /spec/security/reporting-endpoints/ Recommended A response header that names HTTP endpoints to which the browser POSTs structured violation reports — CSP and COOP breaches, permissions-policy violations, deprecations, interventions, and crashes — so you learn what is breaking in the field. [163] input type=checkbox "Mark /.well-known/security.txt done" value="on" [164] link "/.well-known/security.txt" -> /spec/security/security-txt/ Recommended A standard text file at /.well-known/security.txt tells security researchers how to report vulnerabilities. It is cheap to publish and dramatically lowers the bar for responsible disclosure. [165] input type=checkbox "Mark X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff done" value="on" [166] link "X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff" -> /spec/security/x-content-type-options/ Required The nosniff header stops browsers from guessing a response's content type. It blocks a class of attacks where a benign-looking file is interpreted as script or stylesheet. [167] input type=checkbox "Mark Clickjacking protection (frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options) done" value="on" [168] link "Clickjacking protection (frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options)" -> /spec/security/frame-ancestors/ Required Tell browsers who is allowed to embed your pages in an iframe. Use CSP frame-ancestors. X-Frame-Options is the legacy fallback. [169] input type=checkbox "Mark Fetch Metadata request headers done" value="on" [170] link "Fetch Metadata request headers" -> /spec/security/fetch-metadata/ Recommended Read Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode and Sec-Fetch-Dest to reject unwanted cross-site browser requests before a handler runs. Keep ordinary inbound links working and retain other CSRF defences. [171] input type=checkbox "Mark Cross-origin isolation (COOP / COEP / CORP) done" value="on" [172] link "Cross-origin isolation (COOP / COEP / CORP)" -> /spec/security/cross-origin-isolation/ Recommended Three response headers — Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, and Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy — that sever risky cross-window and cross-origin links and defend against side-channel leaks. [173] input type=checkbox "Mark Referrer-Policy done" value="on" [174] link "Referrer-Policy" -> /spec/security/referrer-policy/ Recommended Referrer-Policy controls how much URL information your site leaks when users follow a link or load a subresource. strict-origin-when-cross-origin is the sensible default. [175] input type=checkbox "Mark Permissions-Policy done" value="on" [176] link "Permissions-Policy" -> /spec/security/permissions-policy/ Recommended Permissions-Policy lets you turn off powerful browser features — camera, microphone, geolocation, payment, USB — for your own pages and for any iframes you embed. [177] input type=checkbox "Mark Subresource Integrity (SRI) done" value="on" [178] link "Subresource Integrity (SRI)" -> /spec/security/subresource-integrity/ Recommended SRI adds a cryptographic hash to every third-party script and stylesheet so the browser refuses to run modified files. Essential for any external JS or CSS you depend on. [179] input type=checkbox "Mark Digest Fields (Content-Digest, Repr-Digest and Unencoded-Digest) done" value="on" [180] link "Digest Fields (Content-Digest, Repr-Digest and Unencoded-Digest)" -> /spec/security/digest-fields/ Optional Digest Fields let clients check received bytes. Unencoded-Digest works after decompression, with limited browser support. [181] input type=checkbox "Mark Trusted Types done" value="on" [182] link "Trusted Types" -> /spec/security/trusted-types/ Recommended Trusted Types make the browser reject plain strings at DOM injection sinks like innerHTML, demanding a vetted typed value instead. Switched on with two CSP directives, it neutralises a whole class of DOM-based XSS. [183] input type=checkbox "Mark X-XSS-Protection done" value="on" [184] link "X-XSS-Protection" -> /spec/security/x-xss-protection/ Avoid A dead header that roughly a third of major sites still send. No shipping browser reads it, it was never standardised, and the values people copy-paste were the dangerous ones. Stop sending it and rely on CSP. [185] input type=checkbox "Mark Cookie attributes — Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite done" value="on" [186] link "Cookie attributes — Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite" -> /spec/security/cookie-attributes/ Required Every cookie should be Secure, HttpOnly where possible, and have an explicit SameSite. Use __Host- and __Secure- prefixes for session cookies. [187] input type=checkbox "Mark Clear-Site-Data done" value="on" [188] link "Clear-Site-Data" -> /spec/security/clear-site-data/ Optional Clear-Site-Data lets a response tell the browser to wipe cookies, storage, and caches for your origin. Send it on logout so a shared device keeps nothing behind. [189] input type=checkbox "Mark DNS CAA records done" value="on" [190] link "DNS CAA records" -> /spec/security/caa-records/ Recommended A CAA record tells certificate authorities which of them are allowed to issue certificates for your domain. Cheap to add, blocks a class of mis-issuance attacks. [203] input type=checkbox "Mark /.well-known/openid-configuration done" value="on" [204] link "/.well-known/openid-configuration" -> /spec/well-known/openid-configuration/ Optional A JSON discovery document that describes an OpenID Connect provider's endpoints and capabilities. # Colour contrast
Text and meaningful non-text elements must have enough contrast against their background so people with low vision and people in harsh light can read them.
## What it is
Contrast is the difference in luminance between the foreground (text, icons, control borders) and the background behind them. Luminance is not the same as how different two colours look. A vivid pairing chosen by hue, such as saturated red on green, can sit at almost the same lightness and fail, while an unremarkable dark grey on white passes comfortably. What the ratio measures is lightness against lightness, so picking colours because they clash or feel bold is no guarantee they contrast. WCAG defines minimum ratios that pages must meet so that text remains legible for users with low vision, age-related sight loss, or colour vision deficiencies, and for everyone reading on a glare-filled screen.
## Why it matters
Low contrast is consistently the single most common automated accessibility failure on the web. It locks out users with low vision, makes content unreadable in bright sunlight, and degrades comprehension even for users with average vision. Meeting the contrast minimum is the cheapest, highest-impact accessibility fix you can make to a site.
## How to implement
WCAG 2.2 sets three thresholds you should know:
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) — AA. Body text needs at least 4.5:1 . Large text (18pt, or 14pt bold) needs 3:1 .
1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) — AAA. Body text 7:1 , large text 4.5:1 .
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — AA. Meaningful UI components (input borders, focus rings, icon-only buttons) and graphics needed to understand the content need at least 3:1 against adjacent colours.
Pick colour pairs from a palette that has been checked against these ratios. Use design tokens, not one-off hex values, so a single fix propagates.
:root { --text : #1a1a1a ; /* 16.1:1 on white — comfortable */ --text-muted : #595959 ; /* 7.0:1 on white — passes AAA */ --link : #0b5fff ; /* 6.4:1 on white */ }
APCA (the contrast algorithm being prototyped for WCAG 3) gives a more perceptually accurate score, especially for dark mode. Treat it as a useful second opinion, not a replacement — conformance today is still measured against WCAG 2 ratios.
## Common mistakes
Light grey body text on white (“#aaa on #fff” is 2.3:1 — a clear fail).
Placeholder text used as the only label, set in a low-contrast grey.
Brand-coloured buttons where the label sits below 4.5:1 on the button fill.
Disabled states styled so low that sighted keyboard users cannot see which control has focus.
Text laid over a busy image with no scrim or solid block behind it.
## Verification
Run an automated checker (axe DevTools, WAVE, Lighthouse, Equalize Digital) on every template.
Spot-check the reported failures by hand — automation can miss text on gradients or images.
Test the page in greyscale and in a high-glare environment.

rfaces to match your brand. Use the media attribute to ship one colour for light mode and another for dark mode. [41] input type=checkbox "Mark done" value="on" [42] link "" -> /spec/foundations/color-scheme/ Recommended Tells the browser which colour schemes your page is designed for. Prevents the white flash that dark-mode users see before your CSS loads, and lets the browser style scrollbars, form controls, and the page background to match. [43] input type=checkbox "Mark Open Graph protocol done" value="on" [44] link "Open Graph protocol" -> /spec/foundations/open-graph/ Recommended Open Graph tags control how pages look when shared on social platforms and chat apps. Set og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url, and og:type on every page. [45] input type=checkbox "Mark Feed discovery with rel="alternate" done" value="on" [46] link "Feed discovery with rel="alternate"" -> /spec/foundations/feed-discovery/ Recommended If your site publishes a feed — RSS, Atom, or JSON Feed — announce it in with . Feed readers, agents, and browsers discover it without guessing the URL. [47] input type=checkbox "Mark Feed content hygiene done" value="on" [48] link "Feed content hygiene" -> /spec/foundations/feed-hygiene/ Recommended If you publish a feed, ship it well-formed. Identify the feed inside itself with atom:link rel="self", give every item a stable guid, declare an update cadence with the Syndication module, and validate before deploy. [49] input type=checkbox "Mark Popover API done" value="on" [50] link "Popover API" -> /spec/foundations/popover-api/ Recommended Replace ARIA-puzzled JavaScript modals, menus, and tooltips with a native top-layer primitive that the browser opens, closes, and accessibility-wires for you. [51] input type=checkbox "Mark WebSub — push notification for feeds done" value="on" [52] link "WebSub — push notification for feeds" -> /spec/foundations/websub/ Optional If you publish a feed, advertise a WebSub hub with rel="hub" and rel="self" so subscribers are pushed each update instead of polling for it. Cuts latency to seconds and removes most of the crawl traffic your feed attracts. [53] input type=checkbox "Mark CSS anchor positioning done" value="on" [54] link "CSS anchor positioning" -> /spec/foundations/anchor-positioning/ Recommended Tether tooltips, menus, and popovers to the element that triggers them with pure CSS — no JavaScript positioning library, and it works across overflow and stacking boundaries. [55] input type=checkbox "Mark Balanced text wrapping done" value="on" [56] link "Balanced text wrapping" -> /spec/foundations/text-wrap/ Recommended Let the browser break headings and body copy intelligently with text-wrap: balance and pretty — no orphaned words, no manual line breaks, no layout shift. [57] input type=checkbox "Mark CSS container queries done" value="on" [58] link "CSS container queries" -> /spec/foundations/container-queries/ Recommended Style a component by the space it is actually given with container-type and @container — responsive design that follows the container, not the viewport — and test a container's own custom properties with style queries. [59] input type=checkbox "Mark Invoker commands done" value="on" [60] link "Invoker commands" -> /spec/foundations/invoker-commands/ Optional Wire a button to open a popover, close a dialog, or run a custom action declaratively with command and commandfor — no click handler, no ARIA plumbing. [61] input type=checkbox "Mark _for-sale DNS records done" value="on" [62] link "_for-sale DNS records" -> /spec/foundations/for-sale-dns/ Optional If a domain is genuinely for sale, say so in DNS. A TXT record at _for-sale.example.com advertises it to brokers and availability services without taking the site down or parking it. ## SEO Search visibility — robots.txt, sitemaps, canonicals, structured data. [63] input type=checkbox "Mark robots.txt done" value="on" [64] link "robots.txt" -> /spec/seo/robots-txt/ Recommended A plain-text file at the site root that tells crawlers which paths they may or may not fetch. Standardised in RFC 9309 and supported by every major search engine. [65] input type=checkbox "Mark XML sitemaps done" value="on" [66] link "XML sitemaps" -> /spec/seo/xml-sitemaps/ Recommended An XML file listing the canonical URLs of a site, with optional metadata about when each was last changed. The fastest way to tell a search engine what exists. [67] input type=checkbox "Mark Sitemap index files done" value="on" [68] link "Sitemap index files" -> /spec/seo/sitemap-index/ Recommended A sitemap of sitemaps. Used when a site has more than 50,000 URLs or wants to split sitemaps by content type for cleaner reporting. [69] input type=checkbox "Mark Image and video sitemap extensions done" value="on" [70] link "Image and video sitemap extensions" -> /spec/seo/image-sitemaps/ Optional Optional XML extensions that add image and video metadata to sitemap entries. Useful when media is loaded by JavaScript or hosted on a CDN that crawlers cannot reach by following links. [71] input type=checkbox "Mark URL structure done" value="on" [72] link "URL structure" -> /spec/seo/url-structure/ Recommended URLs are the most stable identifier on the web. Keep them lowercase, hyphenated, descriptive, and shallow. Treat them as a public API for your content. [73] input type=checkbox "Mark Redirects (301/302/308) done" value="on" [74] link "Redirects (301/302/308)" -> /spec/seo/redirects/ Required HTTP redirects send a client from one URL to another. Use 301 or 308 for permanent moves, 302 or 307 for temporary ones, and never chain more than necessary. [75] input type=checkbox "Mark Server-side rendering done" value="on" [76] link "Server-side rendering" -> /spec/seo/server-side-rendering/ Recommended Crawlers, social scrapers, and AI agents index the HTML your server returns. Render your primary content and metadata server-side — via SSR, static generation, or prerendering — so it is in the initial response, not assembled later by client-side JavaScript. [77] input type=checkbox "Mark Soft 404s done" value="on" [78] link "Soft 404s" -> /spec/seo/soft-404/ Avoid A page that looks like a 'not found' message to a user but returns 200 OK to a crawler. Search engines treat soft 404s as a quality problem and often refuse to index them. [79] input type=checkbox "Mark Meta robots and X-Robots-Tag done" value="on" [80] link "Meta robots and X-Robots-Tag" -> /spec/seo/meta-robots/ Required Every page must have an explicit, correct indexing policy — either implicit (default index, follow) on public pages, or an explicit noindex / X-Robots-Tag on staging, admin, thin, or private content. Get this wrong and you either disappear from search or expose what you didn't mean to. [81] input type=checkbox "Mark Heading hierarchy done" value="on" [82] link "Heading hierarchy" -> /spec/seo/heading-hierarchy/ Required Headings describe the sections of a page. They must form a nested outline, never be used for visual styling alone, and never skip levels. [83] input type=checkbox "Mark Internal linking done" value="on" [84] link "Internal linking" -> /spec/seo/internal-linking/ Recommended Links from one page on a site to another. The strongest signal you control for telling crawlers and AI agents what a page is about and how important it is. [85] input type=checkbox "Mark Structured data (JSON-LD) done" value="on" [86] link "Structured data (JSON-LD)" -> /spec/seo/structured-data/ Recommended Machine-readable annotations that describe the content of a page using the schema.org vocabulary. JSON-LD is the format search engines and AI agents expect. [87] input type=checkbox "Mark Breadcrumbs done" value="on" [88] link "Breadcrumbs" -> /spec/seo/breadcrumbs/ Recommended A short trail showing the page's position in the site hierarchy. Visible in the UI for users, marked up as BreadcrumbList JSON-LD for search engines. [89] input type=checkbox "Mark IndexNow done" value="on" [90] link "IndexNow" -> /spec/seo/indexnow/ Optional An open protocol for telling participating search engines that a URL has changed. One HTTP request pushes Bing, Yandex, Naver, and Seznam to recrawl — Google does not participate. ## Accessibility WCAG-aligned rules so people of all abilities can use the site. [91] input type=checkbox "Mark Colour contrast done" value="on" [92] link "Colour contrast" -> /spec/accessibility/color-contrast/ Required Text and meaningful non-text elements must have enough contrast against their background so people with low vision and people in harsh light can read them. [93] input type=checkbox "Mark Automatic contrasting colour done" value="on" [94] link "Automatic contrasting colour" -> /spec/accessibility/contrast-color/ Optional Let the browser pick a legible black or white foreground for a dynamic background with the CSS contrast-color() function, instead of hard-coding colour pairs or computing luminance in JavaScript. [95] input type=checkbox "Mark Forced colours mode done" value="on" [96] link "Forced colours mode" -> /spec/accessibility/forced-colors/ Recommended Respect forced colours mode (Windows High Contrast and similar). The `forced-colors` media feature lets you repair UI the user's palette would otherwise flatten — without overriding their choice. [97] input type=checkbox "Mark Image alt text done" value="on" [98] link "Image alt text" -> /spec/accessibility/image-alt-text/ Required Every element must have an alt attribute. The value describes the image's purpose to screen readers, search engines, and anyone whose image fails to load. [99] input type=checkbox "Mark Form labels done" value="on" [100] link "Form labels" -> /spec/accessibility/form-labels/ Required Every form control needs a programmatically associated label. A placeholder is not a label, and an unlabelled input is unusable for screen-reader and voice-control users. [101] input type=checkbox "Mark Keyboard navigation done" value="on" [102] link "Keyboard navigation" -> /spec/accessibility/keyboard-navigation/ Required Every interactive element on the page must be reachable and operable with a keyboard alone, in a logical order, with no traps that hold focus. [103] input type=checkbox "Mark Visible focus indicators done" value="on" [104] link "Visible focus indicators" -> /spec/accessibility/focus-indicators/ Required Whenever a control receives keyboard focus, the page must show a clear, high-contrast indicator. Removing focus outlines without a replacement is a top accessibility failure. [105] input type=checkbox "Mark Focus not obscured done" value="on" [106] link "Focus not obscured" -> /spec/accessibility/focus-not-obscured/ Recommended A focused control must not be hidden behind a sticky header, cookie banner, or chat widget. WCAG 2.2 added this as a separate criterion because a perfect focus ring is worthless if something is sitting on top of it. [107] input type=checkbox "Mark Skip links done" value="on" [108] link "Skip links" -> /spec/accessibility/skip-links/ Required A 'skip to main content' link as the first focusable element lets keyboard and screen-reader users jump past repeated navigation on every page. [109] input type=checkbox "Mark The inert attribute done" value="on" [110] link "The inert attribute" -> /spec/accessibility/inert-attribute/ Recommended When an overlay is open, the content behind it should be unreachable — not just dimmed. The inert attribute removes a subtree from tab order and the accessibility tree at once, replacing fragile focus-trap JavaScript. [111] input type=checkbox "Mark Semantic HTML and landmarks done" value="on" [112] link "Semantic HTML and landmarks" -> /spec/accessibility/semantic-html/ Required Use the right HTML element for the job. Landmarks like
,
,
, and
let assistive technologies announce structure and skip between regions. [113] input type=checkbox "Mark ARIA — first rule of ARIA done" value="on" [114] link "ARIA — first rule of ARIA" -> /spec/accessibility/aria-usage/ Recommended ARIA can make custom widgets accessible, but the first rule of ARIA is don't use ARIA. Reach for a native HTML element first; add ARIA only when nothing native fits. [115] input type=checkbox "Mark Descriptive link text done" value="on" [116] link "Descriptive link text" -> /spec/accessibility/link-text/ Required Every link's text must describe where it goes. 'Click here' and 'read more' fail screen-reader users who scan a page by jumping from link to link. [117] input type=checkbox "Mark Empty links and buttons done" value="on" [118] link "Empty links and buttons" -> /spec/accessibility/empty-links-buttons/ Avoid A link or button with no accessible name is invisible to screen readers and unreachable for voice control. Icon-only controls without a label are the usual culprit. [119] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessible form errors done" value="on" [120] link "Accessible form errors" -> /spec/accessibility/form-errors/ Required When a form submission fails, errors must be identified in text, associated with the input that caused them, and announced to assistive technology. [121] input type=checkbox "Mark Status messages done" value="on" [122] link "Status messages" -> /spec/accessibility/status-messages/ Recommended When something succeeds, fails or changes without moving focus — a result count, a saved confirmation, a progress update — assistive technology has to be told. Expose it through a live region, or announce it with ariaNotify(). [123] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessible authentication done" value="on" [124] link "Accessible authentication" -> /spec/accessibility/accessible-authentication/ Recommended Let people log in without solving a puzzle, transcribing a code, or memorising anything. Don't block password managers, allow paste, and offer a method that needs no cognitive function test. [125] input type=checkbox "Mark Redundant entry done" value="on" [126] link "Redundant entry" -> /spec/accessibility/redundant-entry/ Recommended Don't make people re-type information they already gave you in the same process. Auto-populate it, or let them pick it from what they entered a step ago. [127] input type=checkbox "Mark Consistent help done" value="on" [128] link "Consistent help" -> /spec/accessibility/consistent-help/ Recommended If you offer help — a contact link, a phone number, a chat widget, an FAQ — put it in the same relative place on every page that has it. Moving it around is the failure. [129] input type=checkbox "Mark Document and parts language done" value="on" [130] link "Document and parts language" -> /spec/accessibility/document-language/ Required Set the page's primary language on and mark any inline content in a different language with its own lang attribute, so screen readers pronounce it correctly. [131] input type=checkbox "Mark Reduced motion done" value="on" [132] link "Reduced motion" -> /spec/accessibility/reduced-motion/ Required Respect the user's `prefers-reduced-motion` setting. Decorative animation, parallax, and autoplay can trigger vestibular distress, migraines, and seizures. [133] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessibility overlays done" value="on" [134] link "Accessibility overlays" -> /spec/accessibility/accessibility-overlays/ Avoid Third-party JavaScript widgets that claim to make a site WCAG-compliant at runtime. They do not work, often harm screen-reader users, and attract lawsuits. [135] input type=checkbox "Mark Captions and transcripts done" value="on" [136] link "Captions and transcripts" -> /spec/accessibility/captions-and-transcripts/ Required Video needs synchronised captions, audio-only content needs a transcript, and visuals that carry meaning need audio description. Auto-captions alone are not enough. [137] input type=checkbox "Mark Accessible data tables done" value="on" [138] link "Accessible data tables" -> /spec/accessibility/data-tables/ Required Tabular data must use real markup with a caption, header cells, and scope attributes so screen readers can announce row and column relationships. [139] input type=checkbox "Mark Touch target size done" value="on" [140] link "Touch target size" -> /spec/accessibility/touch-target-size/ Required Interactive controls must be large enough to tap or click reliably. WCAG 2.2 sets a 24×24 CSS px minimum, with 44×44 CSS px as the enhanced target. [141] input type=checkbox "Mark Dragging movements done" value="on" [142] link "Dragging movements" -> /spec/accessibility/dragging-movements/ Recommended Anything you can drag must also work with a single pointer that never drags. Sliders, sortable lists, and drag-to-pan maps each need a click or tap alternative. [143] input type=checkbox "Mark Hidden until found done" value="on" [144] link "Hidden until found" -> /spec/accessibility/hidden-until-found/ Recommended Use hidden="until-found" for collapsible content so that browser find-in-page, assistive tech, and search engines can still reach the text and auto-expand it. [145] input type=checkbox "Mark Mobile-friendly form inputs done" value="on" [146] link "Mobile-friendly form inputs" -> /spec/accessibility/mobile-form-inputs/ Recommended On a phone, the right input type, inputmode, and enterkeyhint summon the correct on-screen keyboard and a useful Enter key. Keep input text at 16px or larger so iOS Safari doesn't zoom on focus. [147] input type=checkbox "Mark Native interactive elements done" value="on" [148] link "Native interactive elements" -> /spec/accessibility/native-interactive-elements/ Recommended Prefer native HTML interactive elements —

# Colour contrast
Text and meaningful non-text elements must have enough contrast against their background so people with low vision and people in harsh light can read them.
## What it is
Contrast is the difference in luminance between the foreground (text, icons, control borders) and the background behind them. Luminance is not the same as how different two colours look. A vivid pairing chosen by hue, such as saturated red on green, can sit at almost the same lightness and fail, while an unremarkable dark grey on white passes comfortably. What the ratio measures is lightness against lightness, so picking colours because they clash or feel bold is no guarantee they contrast. WCAG defines minimum ratios that pages must meet so that text remains legible for users with low vision, age-related sight loss, or colour vision deficiencies, and for everyone reading on a glare-filled screen.
## Why it matters
Low contrast is consistently the single most common automated accessibility failure on the web. It locks out users with low vision, makes content unreadable in bright sunlight, and degrades comprehension even for users with average vision. Meeting the contrast minimum is the cheapest, highest-impact accessibility fix you can make to a site.
## How to implement
WCAG 2.2 sets three thresholds you should know:
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) — AA. Body text needs at least 4.5:1 . Large text (18pt, or 14pt bold) needs 3:1 .
1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) — AAA. Body text 7:1 , large text 4.5:1 .
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — AA. Meaningful UI components (input borders, focus rings, icon-only buttons) and graphics needed to understand the content need at least 3:1 against adjacent colours.
Pick colour pairs from a palette that has been checked against these ratios. Use design tokens, not one-off hex values, so a single fix propagates.
:root { --text : #1a1a1a ; /* 16.1:1 on white — comfortable */ --text-muted : #595959 ; /* 7.0:1 on white — passes AAA */ --link : #0b5fff ; /* 6.4:1 on white */ }
APCA (the contrast algorithm being prototyped for WCAG 3) gives a more perceptually accurate score, especially for dark mode. Treat it as a useful second opinion, not a replacement — conformance today is still measured against WCAG 2 ratios.
## Common mistakes
Light grey body text on white (“#aaa on #fff” is 2.3:1 — a clear fail).
Placeholder text used as the only label, set in a low-contrast grey.
Brand-coloured buttons where the label sits below 4.5:1 on the button fill.
Disabled states styled so low that sighted keyboard users cannot see which control has focus.
Text laid over a busy image with no scrim or solid block behind it.
## Verification
Run an automated checker (axe DevTools, WAVE, Lighthouse, Equalize Digital) on every template.
Spot-check the reported failures by hand — automation can miss text on gradients or images.
Test the page in greyscale and in a high-glare environment.

[153] input type=checkbox "Mark TLS configuration hardening done" value="on" [154] link "TLS configuration hardening" -> /spec/security/tls-configuration/ Recommended Beyond protocol versions and key exchange: TLS compression off, secure renegotiation only, no unsafe 0-RTT, Extended Main Secret on, server cipher order, SHA-2 signatures, and certificate keys of adequate size. [155] input type=checkbox "Mark HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) done" value="on" [156] link "HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)" -> /spec/security/hsts/ Required HSTS tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS for your domain. [157] input type=checkbox "Mark Mixed content and upgrade-insecure-requests done" value="on" [158] link "Mixed content and upgrade-insecure-requests" -> /spec/security/mixed-content/ Recommended An HTTPS page that loads any subresource over HTTP is mixed content. Serve every subresource over HTTPS, and send the upgrade-insecure-requests CSP directive as a safety net. [159] input type=checkbox "Mark Content Security Policy (CSP) done" value="on" [160] link "Content Security Policy (CSP)" -> /spec/security/content-security-policy/ Recommended A CSP tells browsers which sources of script, style, image, and frame content to trust. A good policy stops most XSS and data-exfiltration attacks dead. [161] input type=checkbox "Mark Reporting API (Reporting-Endpoints) done" value="on" [162] link "Reporting API (Reporting-Endpoints)" -> /spec/security/reporting-endpoints/ Recommended A response header that names HTTP endpoints to which the browser POSTs structured violation reports — CSP and COOP breaches, permissions-policy violations, deprecations, interventions, and crashes — so you learn what is breaking in the field. [163] input type=checkbox "Mark /.well-known/security.txt done" value="on" [164] link "/.well-known/security.txt" -> /spec/security/security-txt/ Recommended A standard text file at /.well-known/security.txt tells security researchers how to report vulnerabilities. It is cheap to publish and dramatically lowers the bar for responsible disclosure. [165] input type=checkbox "Mark X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff done" value="on" [166] link "X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff" -> /spec/security/x-content-type-options/ Required The nosniff header stops browsers from guessing a response's content type. [167] input type=checkbox "Mark Clickjacking protection (frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options) done" value="on" [168] link "Clickjacking protection (frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options)" -> /spec/security/frame-ancestors/ Required Tell browsers who is allowed to embed your pages in an iframe. [169] input type=checkbox "Mark Fetch Metadata request headers done" value="on" [170] link "Fetch Metadata request headers" -> /spec/security/fetch-metadata/ Recommended Read Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode and Sec-Fetch-Dest to reject unwanted cross-site browser requests before a handler runs. [171] input type=checkbox "Mark Cross-origin isolation (COOP / COEP / CORP) done" value="on" [172] link "Cross-origin isolation (COOP / COEP / CORP)" -> /spec/security/cross-origin-isolation/ Recommended Three response headers — Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, and Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy — that sever risky cross-window and cross-origin links and defend against side-channel leaks. [181] input type=checkbox "Mark Trusted Types done" value="on" [182] link "Trusted Types" -> /spec/security/trusted-types/ Recommended Trusted Types make the browser reject plain strings at DOM injection sinks like innerHTML, demanding a vetted typed value instead. # Colour contrast

> Text and meaningful non-text elements must have enough contrast against their background so people with low vision and people in harsh light can read them.

## What it is

Contrast is the difference in luminance between the foreground (text, icons, control borders) and the background behind them. Luminance is not the same as how different two colours look. A vivid pairing chosen by hue, such as saturated red on green, can sit at almost the same lightness and fail, while an unremarkable dark grey on white passes comfortably. What the ratio measures is lightness against lightness, so picking colours because they clash or feel bold is no guarantee they contrast. WCAG defines minimum ratios that pages must meet so that text remains legible for users with low vision, age-related sight loss, or colour vision deficiencies, and for everyone reading on a glare-filled screen.

## Why it matters

Low contrast is consistently the single most common automated accessibility failure on the web. It locks out users with low vision, makes content unreadable in bright sunlight, and degrades comprehension even for users with average vision. Meeting the contrast minimum is the cheapest, highest-impact accessibility fix you can make to a site.

## How to implement

WCAG 2.2 sets three thresholds you should know:

- **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) — AA.** Body text needs at least **4.5:1**. Large text (18pt, or 14pt bold) needs **3:1**.
- **1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) — AAA.** Body text **7:1**, large text **4.5:1**.
- **1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — AA.** Meaningful UI components (input borders, focus rings, icon-only buttons) and graphics needed to understand the content need at least **3:1** against adjacent colours.

Pick colour pairs from a palette that has been checked against these ratios. Use design tokens, not one-off hex values, so a single fix propagates.

:root {

# HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)
HSTS tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS for your domain. Send max-age with includeSubDomains — but skip the preload list, which its own operator now discourages.
## What it is
HTTP Strict Transport Security, defined in RFC 6797, is a response header that tells the browser: from now on, never speak HTTP to this host — only HTTPS. The browser remembers the instruction for the duration of max-age and refuses plain HTTP even if the user types it, clicks a stale link, or has DNS hijacked.
Strict-Transport-Security : max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
## Why it matters
A 301 redirect from HTTP to HTTPS only protects the second request. The first request — and any cookies sent with it — already left the device in plain text. HSTS closes that gap. It also defends against active downgrade attacks where a network attacker strips the redirect and proxies the connection.
Without HSTS, every typed URL, bookmark, and external link to http://example.com is a moment when an attacker on the network can intercept the session.
## How to implement
Send the header on every HTTPS response. Browsers ignore it on plain HTTP.
Directives:
max-age=<seconds> — required. How long the browser remembers. Start short (a few hours) to verify, then raise to two years ( 63072000 ) before preloading.
includeSubDomains — applies the policy to every subdomain. Audit them first (see below).
preload — opts in to the browser preload list. No longer recommended for most sites — the list’s own operator now advises against it (see below), so leave it off unless you have a specific reason.
Recommended production header:
Strict-Transport-Security : max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
This site sends exactly that — max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains , no preload — from

### Preloading is no longer recommended
The historic advice was to add preload and submit the domain to

, hard-coding HTTPS-only into browsers so that even a first visit on a fresh device is protected. That guidance has changed. Modern browsers (Chrome, Safari) now auto-upgrade every HTTP navigation to HTTPS regardless of any HSTS policy, so preloading only helps in the narrow case where that upgrade fails against an active attacker. The list operator now states it plainly: “ HSTS preloading is not recommended. ” The commitment, meanwhile, is heavy — removal from the list takes months and applies to every subdomain. For nearly all sites, a strong max-age with includeSubDomains is the right stopping point; skip preload .
## Common mistakes
Sending HSTS over HTTP. Browsers must ignore it. Send it on HTTPS responses only.
Setting includeSubDomains without auditing subdomains. Every subdomain — including internal tools, staging, and legacy services — must work over HTTPS. If dev.example.com is HTTP-only, you have just broken it.

Adding preload reflexively. The preload list is now discouraged by its own operator, and getting a domain off it takes months. Ship HSTS without it unless you have a specific reason.

HSTS is a commitment, not a switch. Plan the rollback path before you ship.

Setting includeSubDomains without auditing subdomains. Every subdomain — including internal tools, staging, and legacy services — must work over HTTPS. If dev.example.com is HTTP-only, you have just broken it.
Setting max-age=0 by accident. That removes HSTS. Useful when rolling back, dangerous when copied from a tutorial.
Adding preload reflexively. The preload list is now discouraged by its own operator, and getting a domain off it takes months. Ship HSTS without it unless you have a specific reason.
## Verification
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i strict-transport-security should return the header.
In Chrome DevTools, the Security panel shows the HSTS state for the current site.
HSTS is a commitment, not a switch. Plan the rollback path before you ship.

# HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)
HSTS tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS for your domain. Send max-age with includeSubDomains — but skip the preload list, which its own operator now discourages.
## What it is
HTTP Strict Transport Security, defined in RFC 6797, is a response header that tells the browser: from now on, never speak HTTP to this host — only HTTPS. The browser remembers the instruction for the duration of max-age and refuses plain HTTP even if the user types it, clicks a stale link, or has DNS hijacked.
Strict-Transport-Security : max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
## Why it matters
A 301 redirect from HTTP to HTTPS only protects the second request. The first request — and any cookies sent with it — already left the device in plain text. HSTS closes that gap. It also defends against active downgrade attacks where a network attacker strips the redirect and proxies the connection.
Without HSTS, every typed URL, bookmark, and external link to http://example.com is a moment when an attacker on the network can intercept the session.
## How to implement
Send the header on every HTTPS response. Browsers ignore it on plain HTTP.
Directives:
max-age=<seconds> — required. How long the browser remembers. Start short (a few hours) to verify, then raise to two years ( 63072000 ) before preloading.
includeSubDomains — applies the policy to every subdomain. Audit them first (see below).
preload — opts in to the browser preload list. No longer recommended for most sites — the list’s own operator now advises against it (see below), so leave it off unless you have a specific reason.
Recommended production header:
Strict-Transport-Security : max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
This site sends exactly that — max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains , no preload — from
[25] link "public/_headers" -> https://github.com/jdevalk/specification.website/blob/main/public/_headers
.
### Preloading is no longer recommended
The historic advice was to add preload and submit the domain to
[26] link "the preload list" -> https://hstspreload.org/
, hard-coding HTTPS-only into browsers so that even a first visit on a fresh device is protected. That guidance has changed. Modern browsers (Chrome, Safari) now auto-upgrade every HTTP navigation to HTTPS regardless of any HSTS policy, so preloading only helps in the narrow case where that upgrade fails against an active attacker. The list operator now states it plainly: “ HSTS preloading is not recommended. ” The commitment, meanwhile, is heavy — removal from the list takes months and applies to every subdomain. For nearly all sites, a strong max-age with includeSubDomains is the right stopping point; skip preload .
## Common mistakes
Sending HSTS over HTTP. Browsers must ignore it. Send it on HTTPS responses only.
Setting includeSubDomains without auditing subdomains. Every subdomain — including internal tools, staging, and legacy services — must work over HTTPS. If dev.example.com is HTTP-only, you have just broken it.
Setting max-age=0 by accident. That removes HSTS. Useful when rolling back, dangerous when copied from a tutorial.
Adding preload reflexively. The preload list is now discouraged by its own operator, and getting a domain off it takes months. Ship HSTS without it unless you have a specific reason.
## Verification
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i strict-transport-security should return the header.
In Chrome DevTools, the Security panel shows the HSTS state for the current site.
HSTS is a commitment, not a switch. Plan the rollback path before you ship.

# HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)

> HSTS tells browsers to only ever use HTTPS for your domain. Send max-age with includeSubDomains — but skip the preload list, which its own operator now discourages.

## What it is

HTTP Strict Transport Security, defined in RFC 6797, is a response header that tells the browser: from now on, never speak HTTP to this host — only HTTPS. The browser remembers the instruction for the duration of `max-age` and refuses plain HTTP even if the user types it, clicks a stale link, or has DNS hijacked.

```http
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
```

## Why it matters

A 301 redirect from HTTP to HTTPS only protects the second request. The first request — and any cookies sent with it — already left the device in plain text. HSTS closes that gap. It also defends against active downgrade attacks where a network attacker strips the redirect and proxies the connection.

Without HSTS, every typed URL, bookmark, and external link to `http://example.com` is a moment when an attacker on the network can intercept the session.

## How to implement

Send the header on every HTTPS response. Browsers ignore it on plain HTTP.

Directives:

- **`max-age=<seconds>`** — required. How long the browser remembers. Start short (a few hours) to verify, then raise to two years (`63072000`) before preloading.
- **`includeSubDomains`** — applies the policy to every subdomain. Audit them first (see below).
- **`preload`** — opts in to the browser preload list. **No longer recommended** for most sites — the list's own operator now advises against it (see below), so leave it off unless you have a specific reason.

Recommended production header:

```http
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
```

This site sends exactly that — `max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains`, no `preload` — from [`public/_headers`](https://github.com/jdevalk/specification.website/blob/main/public/_headers).

### Preloading is no longer recommended

The historic advice was to add `preload` and submit the domain to [the preload list](https://hstspreload.org/), hard-coding HTTPS-only into browsers so that even a first visit on a fresh device is protected. That guidance has changed. Modern browsers (Chrome, Safari) now auto-upgrade every HTTP navigation to HTTPS regardless of any HSTS policy, so preloading only helps in the narrow case where that upgrade fails against an active attacker. The list operator now states it plainly: "**HSTS preloading is not recommended.**" The commitment, meanwhile, is heavy — removal from the list takes months and applies to every subdomain. For nearly all sites, a strong `max-age` with `includeSubDomains` is the right stopping point; skip `preload`.

## Common mistakes

- **Sending HSTS over HTTP.** Browsers must ignore it. Send it on HTTPS responses only.
- **Setting `includeSubDomains` without auditing subdomains.** Every subdomain — including internal tools, staging, and legacy services — must work over HTTPS. If `dev.example.com` is HTTP-only, you have just broken it.
- **Setting `max-age=0` by accident.** That removes HSTS. Useful when rolling back, dangerous when copied from a tutorial.
- **Adding `preload` reflexively.** The preload list is now discouraged by its own operator, and getting a domain off it takes months. Ship HSTS without it unless you have a specific reason.

## Verification

- `curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i strict-transport-security` should return the header.
- In Chrome DevTools, the Security panel shows the HSTS state for the current site.

HSTS is a commitment, not a switch. Plan the rollback path before you ship.

# Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS)
Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Hit LCP ≤ 2.5s, INP ≤ 200ms, and CLS ≤ 0.1 at the 75th percentile of real users.
## What it is
Core Web Vitals are three user-centric metrics that Google uses to score the quality of a page experience:
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — time from navigation start until the largest visible element is painted. Measures loading.
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — the slowest interaction the user has with the page, from input to the next frame. Measures responsiveness.
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — the sum of unexpected layout shift scores during the page’s lifecycle. Measures visual stability.
The targets, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads across mobile and desktop:
Metric
Good
Needs improvement
Poor
LCP
≤ 2.5s
≤ 4.0s
> 4.0s
INP
≤ 200ms
≤ 500ms
> 500ms
CLS
≤ 0.1
≤ 0.25
> 0.25
## Why it matters
The numbers that count are field data from real users, captured in the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) and surfaced in Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, and the CrUX API. Lab data from Lighthouse is a useful proxy but not the score Google ranks on.
Slow pages lose users. Field studies consistently show conversion, bounce rate, and session depth all degrading sharply past the “good” thresholds. Core Web Vitals are also a confirmed Google ranking signal as part of page experience.
## How to implement
LCP — identify the LCP element (usually a hero image or heading) and make it arrive fast. Serve it from the origin, preload it, avoid lazy-loading it, and keep it out of client-rendered components.
INP — break up long JavaScript tasks, defer non-critical work, and avoid heavy work in event handlers. Inside a long task, await scheduler.yield() between chunks so the browser can process input — the continuation runs at boosted priority, so your work finishes before other queued tasks. To schedule new low-priority work, use scheduler.postTask(fn, {priority: 'background'}) or requestIdleCallback . Audit third-party scripts.
CLS — set explicit width and height on images, iframes, and video. Reserve space for ads and embeds. Avoid inserting content above existing content. Preload fonts to reduce FOUT swaps.
## Common mistakes
Optimising lab scores while field data stays red.
Treating LCP as “first paint” — it is the largest element, often well into the page.
Lazy-loading the LCP image. It must load eagerly.
Measuring INP only on the homepage — interaction-heavy pages such as forms and search results are usually the worst offenders.
## Verification
Check field data in

— it pulls from CrUX.
Use the

to send real-user metrics to your analytics.
In Chrome DevTools, the Performance panel flags LCP, INP, and layout shifts.

# Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS)
Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Hit LCP ≤ 2.5s, INP ≤ 200ms, and CLS ≤ 0.1 at the 75th percentile of real users.
## What it is
Core Web Vitals are three user-centric metrics that Google uses to score the quality of a page experience:
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — time from navigation start until the largest visible element is painted. Measures loading.
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — the slowest interaction the user has with the page, from input to the next frame. Measures responsiveness.
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — the sum of unexpected layout shift scores during the page’s lifecycle. Measures visual stability.
The targets, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads across mobile and desktop:
Metric
Good
Needs improvement
Poor
LCP
≤ 2.5s
≤ 4.0s
> 4.0s
INP
≤ 200ms
≤ 500ms
> 500ms
CLS
≤ 0.1
≤ 0.25
> 0.25
## Why it matters
The numbers that count are field data from real users, captured in the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) and surfaced in Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, and the CrUX API. Lab data from Lighthouse is a useful proxy but not the score Google ranks on.
Slow pages lose users. Field studies consistently show conversion, bounce rate, and session depth all degrading sharply past the “good” thresholds. Core Web Vitals are also a confirmed Google ranking signal as part of page experience.
## How to implement
LCP — identify the LCP element (usually a hero image or heading) and make it arrive fast. Serve it from the origin, preload it, avoid lazy-loading it, and keep it out of client-rendered components.
INP — break up long JavaScript tasks, defer non-critical work, and avoid heavy work in event handlers. Inside a long task, await scheduler.yield() between chunks so the browser can process input — the continuation runs at boosted priority, so your work finishes before other queued tasks. To schedule new low-priority work, use scheduler.postTask(fn, {priority: 'background'}) or requestIdleCallback . Audit third-party scripts.
CLS — set explicit width and height on images, iframes, and video. Reserve space for ads and embeds. Avoid inserting content above existing content. Preload fonts to reduce FOUT swaps.
## Common mistakes
Optimising lab scores while field data stays red.
Treating LCP as “first paint” — it is the largest element, often well into the page.
Lazy-loading the LCP image. It must load eagerly.
Measuring INP only on the homepage — interaction-heavy pages such as forms and search results are usually the worst offenders.
## Verification
Check field data in

— it pulls from CrUX.
Use the

to send real-user metrics to your analytics.
In Chrome DevTools, the Performance panel flags LCP, INP, and layout shifts.

Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Hit LCP ≤ 2.5s, INP ≤ 200ms, and CLS ≤ 0.1 at the 75th percentile of real users.
## What it is
Core Web Vitals are three user-centric metrics that Google uses to score the quality of a page experience:
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — time from navigation start until the largest visible element is painted. Measures loading.
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — the slowest interaction the user has with the page, from input to the next frame. Measures responsiveness.
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — the sum of unexpected layout shift scores during the page’s lifecycle. Measures visual stability.
The targets, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads across mobile and desktop:
Metric
Good

## Why it matters
The numbers that count are field data from real users, captured in the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) and surfaced in Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, and the CrUX API. Lab data from Lighthouse is a useful proxy but not the score Google ranks on.
Slow pages lose users. Field studies consistently show conversion, bounce rate, and session depth all degrading sharply past the “good” thresholds. Core Web Vitals are also a confirmed Google ranking signal as part of page experience.
## How to implement
LCP — identify the LCP element (usually a hero image or heading) and make it arrive fast. Serve it from the origin, preload it, avoid lazy-loading it, and keep it out of client-rendered components.
INP — break up long JavaScript tasks, defer non-critical work, and avoid heavy work in event handlers. Inside a long task, await scheduler.yield() between chunks so the browser can process input — the continuation runs at boosted priority, so your work finishes before other queued tasks. To schedule new low-priority work, use scheduler.postTask(fn, {priority: 'background'}) or requestIdleCallback . Audit third-party scripts.
CLS — set explicit width and height on images, iframes, and video. Reserve space for ads and embeds. Avoid inserting content above existing content. Preload fonts to reduce FOUT swaps.
## Common mistakes
Optimising lab scores while field data stays red.
Treating LCP as “first paint” — it is the largest element, often well into the page.
Lazy-loading the LCP image. It must load eagerly.
Measuring INP only on the homepage — interaction-heavy pages such as forms and search results are usually the worst offenders.
